topics.title: Renal physiology
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 1-3; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 3-6; Harrison 22e Ch. 310

mustKnow.fact: Glomerular filtration rate is determined by Starling forces across glomerular capillaries, where normal net ultrafiltration pressure of approximately 10 to 15 mmHg is driven by glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure opposing plasma oncotic pressure and Bowman space hydrostatic pressure.

Tubuloglomerular feedback operates via macula densa cells sensing sodium chloride delivery through apical NKCC2 cotransporters, releasing adenosine to constrict afferent arterioles and decrease GFR when distal tubular flow rises.
Renal autoregulation maintains renal blood flow and GFR relatively constant across mean arterial pressures ranging from 80 to 180 mmHg via myogenic tone and tubuloglomerular feedback.

The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs approximately 65% to 70% of filtered sodium and water, primarily coupled to sodium-hydrogen antiporter 3 (NHE3) and apical sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2).
The thick ascending limb of Henle generates the medullary hyperosmolar gradient via the apical NKCC2 cotransporter without water reabsorption, establishing the countercurrent multiplier mechanism.
The early distal convoluted tubule reabsorbs 5% to 7% of filtered sodium via the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride cotransporter NCC, while remaining impermeable to water.

Cortical collecting duct principal cells mediate electrogenic sodium reabsorption via epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) stimulated by aldosterone, creating a lumen-negative potential driving potassium and proton secretion.

Free water clearance is positive in diuresis when urine osmolality is lower than plasma osmolality, and negative during antidiuresis mediated by arginine vasopressin-induced aquaporin-2 translocation to principal cell apical membranes.

topics.title: Urinalysis, haematuria and proteinuria
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 4; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 25; Harrison 22e Ch. 311

mustKnow.fact: Acanthocytes (ring-shaped red cells with blebs or vesicle projections) exceeding 5% of excreted red cells or true red blood cell casts are virtually pathognomonic for glomerular haematuria.
Muddy brown granular casts composed of sloughed necrotic tubular epithelial cells and Tamm-Horsfall mucoprotein confirm the diagnosis of acute tubular necrosis in acute kidney injury.
Broad waxy casts with blunt fractured ends signify marked tubular dilation and stasis characteristic of advanced chronic kidney disease.

Urine dipstick protein detection uses tetrabromphenol blue, which is sensitive primarily to albumin and fails to detect low concentrations of immunoglobulin light chains (Bence Jones proteinuria) or tubular microproteins.

Spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) categorises albuminuria into A1 (normal to mildly increased, less than 30 mg/g), A2 (moderately increased, 30 to 300 mg/g), and A3 (severely increased, greater than 300 mg/g).

Orthostatic (postural) proteinuria is defined as benign proteinuria present exclusively in the upright position and completely absent in first-morning recumbent urine samples, typically remaining under 1 g per day in young individuals.

Tubular proteinuria is characterised by excretion of low-molecular-weight proteins like beta-2 microglobulin, alpha-1 microglobulin, and retinol-binding protein due to impaired proximal tubular endocytosis without nephrotic-range albuminuria.

Envelope-shaped calcium oxalate dihydrate crystals and dumbbell-shaped monohydrate crystals in acidic urine suggest hyperoxaluria or ethylene glycol poisoning, whereas coffin-lid magnesium ammonium phosphate crystals occur in Proteus infection.

topics.title: GFR estimation and kidney biomarkers
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 4; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 24; Harrison 22e Ch. 310

mustKnow.fact: The CKD-EPI 2021 race-free creatinine estimating equation eliminates the race coefficient to provide standardized and unbiased GFR estimation across diverse populations without sacrificing diagnostic performance.

Serum cystatin C is freely filtered by glomeruli and catabolized by proximal tubular cells without significant tubular secretion, making cystatin C-based eGFR unaffected by muscle mass, dietary protein intake, or sarcopenia.

Plasma clearance of iohexol, inulin, or 51Cr-EDTA represents the gold-standard reference method for measured GFR (mGFR) in clinical trials and confirmatory assessment when estimating equations are unreliable.

Trimethoprim, cimetidine, cobicistat, and dolutegravir competitively inhibit organic cation transporter 2 (OCT2) and MATE1-mediated proximal tubular creatinine secretion, elevating serum creatinine without reducing true GFR.

Cockcroft-Gault formula estimates creatinine clearance utilizing age, weight, and serum creatinine, requiring multiplication by 0.85 in female patients, and is still widely used in legacy drug dosing protocols.

Neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL) rises in urine and plasma within 2 to 4 hours following acute ischemic or toxic proximal tubular injury, serving as an early structural biomarker preceding creatinine elevation.

Kidney injury molecule-1 (KIM-1) is a transmembrane glycoprotein whose ectodomain is cleaved into urine specifically from dedifferentiated proximal tubular epithelial cells during ischemic or toxic necrosis.

The cell cycle arrest biomarker panel combining urinary TIMP-2 and IGFBP7 (NephroCheck) assesses cellular stress, where an index exceeding 0.3 (ng/mL)2/1000 predicts imminent moderate to severe AKI within 12 hours.

topics.title: Kidney imaging and biopsy
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 5-6; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 26-27; Harrison 22e Ch. 312

mustKnow.fact: Renal ultrasound demonstrates normal bipolar renal length of 10 to 12 cm with cortical echogenicity normally equal to or less than adjacent liver parenchyma, while increased echogenicity signifies medical renal parenchymal disease.

Renal resistive index (RI) measured by spectral Doppler ultrasound is calculated as (peak systolic velocity - end diastolic velocity) / peak systolic velocity, where values exceeding 0.70 indicate elevated intrarenal vascular impedance.

Technetium-99m DMSA (dimercaptosuccinic acid) binds to proximal tubular cells and provides cortical imaging to detect renal scarring, while Tc-99m MAG3 is cleared by tubular secretion, optimal for dynamic renography in obstruction.

Gadolinium-based contrast agents in patients with severe kidney disease (eGFR < 30 mL/min/1.73m2 or on dialysis) carry a risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF), highest with linear non-ionic chelate formulations.

Absolute contraindications to percutaneous native kidney biopsy include uncorrected bleeding diathesis, severe refractory hypertension, solitary functioning native kidney (relative), and active renal or perinephric infection.

A diagnostically adequate percutaneous renal biopsy specimen requires at least 8 to 10 glomeruli for light microscopy and at least 1 to 2 glomeruli each for immunofluorescence and electron microscopy examination.

Post-biopsy arteriovenous fistulas develop in up to 10% of cases, diagnosed by high-velocity low-resistance turbulent jet on color Doppler, with the vast majority resolving spontaneously within 1 to 2 years.

Electron microscopy in renal biopsy is mandatory for evaluating glomerular basement membrane thickness, podocyte foot process effacement in minimal change disease, and ultrastructural subendothelial or subepithelial deposits.

topics.title: Disorders of sodium and water
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 8-10; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 15; Harrison 22e Ch. 313

mustKnow.fact: Severe acute symptomatic hyponatremia is treated immediately with a 100 to 150 mL intravenous bolus of 3% hypertonic saline over 10 to 20 minutes, repeatable up to twice to raise serum sodium by 4 to 6 mmol/L and abort cerebral edema and seizures.

To prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome, chronic hyponatremia correction must strictly not exceed 8 mmol/L in any 24-hour period, or 6 mmol/L in high-risk patients with malnutrition, alcoholism, or hypokalemia.

Overcorrection of hyponatremia with rapid water diuresis is promptly reversed using desmopressin (dDAVP 1 to 2 mcg parenterally) combined with 5% dextrose in water infusion to re-lower serum sodium below target limits.

Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) requires hypotonic hyponatremia (plasma osmolality < 275 mOsm/kg), inappropriate urine concentration (urine osmolality > 100 mOsm/kg), elevated urine sodium (> 30 mmol/L), and clinical euvolemia with normal thyroid and adrenal function.

Tolvaptan is an oral selective vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist indicated for clinically significant euvolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia, requiring initiation in-hospital without fluid restriction and limited to 30 days due to hepatotoxicity risk.

Pseudohyponatremia occurs when severe hyperlipidemia or hyperproteinemia (multiple myeloma) expands the non-aqueous plasma fraction, yielding artifactually low sodium on indirect ion-selective electrodes while direct potentiometry and plasma osmolality remain normal.

Free water deficit in hypernatremia is calculated as Total Body Water multiplied by [(serum sodium / 140) - 1], where TBW is estimated as 0.6 in young men, 0.5 in young women and elderly men, and 0.45 in elderly women.

Beer potomania and tea-and-toast syndrome cause profound hyponatremia due to extremely low solute intake (< 250 mOsm/day), which limits maximum free water excretion despite maximally suppressed vasopressin levels.

topics.title: Disorders of potassium
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 11; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 16; Harrison 22e Ch. 314

mustKnow.fact: Intravenous 10% calcium gluconate (10 to 20 mL over 2 to 5 minutes) immediately stabilizes the myocardial resting membrane potential against hyperkalemic cardiotoxicity without altering serum potassium concentrations.

Hyperkalemia ECG progression follows a typical sequence: tall peaked symmetrical T waves (K > 5.5 mmol/L), prolonged PR interval and flattened P waves (K > 6.5 mmol/L), QRS widening and bundle branch blocks (K > 7.0 mmol/L), culminating in a sine-wave pattern and ventricular fibrillation.

Insulin (10 units regular IV) with 50 mL of 50% dextrose shifts potassium intracellularly within 15 to 30 minutes by activating skeletal muscle sodium-potassium ATPase pumps, lowering serum potassium by 0.5 to 1.2 mmol/L.

Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (SZC) is a non-absorbed inorganic cation exchanger that traps potassium in exchange for sodium throughout the gastrointestinal tract, demonstrating onset of potassium lowering within 1 hour.

Patiromer is a non-absorbed spherical polymer that exchanges calcium for potassium in the distal colon, effective for enabling long-term guideline-directed RAAS inhibitor continuation in chronic kidney disease and heart failure.

Urine potassium-to-creatinine ratio (UK/UCr) differentiates renal from non-renal potassium loss, where a ratio less than 1.5 to 2.0 mmol/mmol (or 15 to 20 mEq/g creatinine) indicates appropriate renal conservation and extrarenal wasting.

Hypokalemic periodic paralysis presents with episodic flaccid muscle paralysis provoked by high-carbohydrate meals or rest after exertion, linked to mutations in skeletal muscle voltage-gated calcium (CACNA1S) or sodium (SCN4A) channels.

Pseudohyperkalemia is caused by in vitro potassium leakage from hemolyzed erythrocytes, severe thrombocytosis (> 500,000/mcL), or profound leukocytosis (> 50,000/mcL), confirmed by comparing normal plasma potassium against elevated serum potassium.

topics.title: Acid-base disorders
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 12; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 17; Harrison 22e Ch. 315

mustKnow.fact: Serum anion gap is calculated as [Na+] - ([Cl-] + [HCO3-]), where the normal range of 8 to 12 mmol/L must be adjusted for hypoalbuminemia by adding 2.5 mmol/L for every 1.0 g/dL drop in serum albumin below 4.0 g/dL.

Winter formula predicts compensatory arterial PCO2 in metabolic acidosis as (1.5 x [HCO3-]) + 8 +/- 2; a measured PCO2 higher indicates concomitant respiratory acidosis, while a lower value signifies concurrent respiratory alkalosis.

The delta-delta ratio (delta AG / delta HCO3-) distinguishes mixed high anion gap and non-anion gap metabolic acidosis: a ratio < 0.8 indicates mixed HAGMA and NAGMA, while a ratio > 2.0 suggests concurrent metabolic alkalosis or pre-existing hyperbicarbonatemia.

Osmolar gap exceeding 10 mOsm/kg H2O (calculated as Measured Osmolality minus [2 x Na + Glucose/18 + BUN/2.8]) strongly indicates ingestion of low-molecular-weight toxic alcohols including ethylene glycol, methanol, or isopropanol.

Urine anion gap calculated as [Na+] + [K+] - [Cl-] differentiates normal anion gap metabolic acidosis: a negative value indicates appropriate renal ammonium excretion (gastrointestinal bicarbonate loss), whereas a positive value signifies impaired renal acidification.

Chloride-responsive metabolic alkalosis exhibits urine chloride < 20 mmol/L and responds to intravenous 0.9% saline infusion (vomiting, nasogastric suction, prior diuretic use), whereas chloride-resistant alkalosis exhibits urine chloride > 20 mmol/L and persistent mineralocorticoid excess.

In acute respiratory acidosis, plasma bicarbonate rises by 1 mmol/L for every 10 mmHg elevation in PCO2, whereas in chronic respiratory acidosis renal compensation elevates bicarbonate by 3.5 to 4 mmol/L per 10 mmHg PCO2 increase.

Stewart physicochemical approach evaluates acid-base balance via three independent variables: strong ion difference (SID), total weak non-volatile acids (ATOT), and partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PCO2).

topics.title: Renal tubular acidosis
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 13; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 17; Harrison 22e Ch. 315

mustKnow.fact: Distal renal tubular acidosis (Type 1 RTA) is caused by impaired alpha-intercalated cell H+-ATPase or chloride-bicarbonate exchanger AE1 function, characterized by inability to acidify urine below pH 5.5 despite systemic acidemia.
Type 1 RTA causes recurrent nephrolithiasis and medullary nephrocalcinosis due to the combination of alkaline urine pH, hypercalciuria from bone buffering, and severe hypocitraturia.

Proximal renal tubular acidosis (Type 2 RTA) arises from defective proximal tubule bicarbonate reabsorption (sodium-bicarbonate cotransporter NBCe1), manifesting with fractional excretion of bicarbonate > 15% during bicarbonate loading.
Type 2 RTA commonly presents as a component of Fanconi syndrome with renal glucosuria at normal glycemia, generalized aminoaciduria, hyperuricosuria, and hypophosphatemic rickets or osteomalacia.

Type 4 RTA (hyperkalemic RTA) is caused by aldosterone deficiency or resistance, marked by hyperkalemia, normal anion gap metabolic acidosis, and urine pH < 5.5, commonly seen in diabetic nephropathy (hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism).

Urine osmolal gap calculated as Measured Urine Osmolality - [2 x (Na + K) + Urea/2.8 + Glucose/18] accurately estimates urinary ammonium concentration, where a value < 40 mOsm/kg confirms defective distal acidification.
Sjogren syndrome, systemic lupus erythematosus, and autoimmune thyroiditis are the most frequent secondary autoimmune etiologies of classical adult distal Type 1 RTA.
Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, ifosfamide, and platinum compounds induce toxic proximal mitochondrial tubulopathy leading to acquired adult Fanconi syndrome and proximal Type 2 RTA.

modules.name: Disorders of calcium, phosphate and magnesium

topics.title: Disorders of calcium, phosphate and magnesium
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 14; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 18; Harrison 22e Ch. 316

mustKnow.fact: Severe hypercalcemia (serum calcium > 14 mg/dL or 3.5 mmol/L) requires urgent aggressive intravascular expansion with 0.9% isotonic saline (200 to 300 mL/h) followed by intravenous zoledronic acid (4 mg) or denosumab.

Fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23) produced by osteocytes acts with its co-receptor alpha-Klotho on proximal renal tubules to downregulate NaPi-2a and NaPi-2c cotransporters, promoting phosphaturia and suppressing 1-alpha-hydroxylase.

Severe hypophosphatemia (< 1.0 mg/dL or 0.3 mmol/L) during refeeding syndrome causes critical intracellular ATP depletion, manifesting as diaphragmatic weakness, rhabdomyolysis, erythrocyte hemolysis, and cardiac failure.

Hyperphosphatemia in acute kidney injury and tumor lysis syndrome binds circulating ionized calcium, producing metastatic soft-tissue calcification and nephrocalcinosis when the calcium-phosphate product exceeds 55 mg2/dL2.

Hypomagnesemia impairs parathyroid hormone secretion and induces peripheral end-organ PTH resistance, causing refractory hypokalemia and hypocalcemia that cannot be corrected until magnesium is repleted.
Long-term proton pump inhibitor (PPI) therapy causes profound hypomagnesemia via downregulation of the active intestinal magnesium channel transient receptor potential melastatin 6 (TRPM6).

Familial hypomagnesemia with hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis (FHHNC) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in claudin-16 (paracellin-1) or claudin-19, disrupting paracellular divalent cation reabsorption in the thick ascending limb.

Fractional excretion of magnesium (FEMg) distinguishes renal from extrarenal magnesium wasting in hypomagnesemia, where FEMg > 4% (or 24-hour urine magnesium > 24 mg) indicates inappropriate renal tubular wasting.

topics.title: Diuretics and diuretic resistance
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 15; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 53; Harrison 22e Ch. 317

mustKnow.fact: Loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide, torsemide) reversibly inhibit the apical Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2) in the thick ascending limb of Henle, eliminating the lumen-positive potential and promoting excretion of Na+, Cl-, K+, Ca2+, and Mg2+.
The oral bioavailability of furosemide is highly erratic (10% to 90%, averaging 50%), whereas bumetanide and torsemide exhibit predictable oral bioavailability exceeding 80% to 90%.

Sequential nephron blockade combines a loop diuretic with a thiazide or thiazide-like diuretic (metolazone, chlorthalidone, intravenous chlorothiazide) to overcome distal tubular hypertrophy and sodium avid reabsorption in refractory diuretic resistance.

The CLICK trial established that the thiazide-like diuretic chlorthalidone significantly reduces 24-hour ambulatory systolic blood pressure and urinary albumin excretion in patients with advanced stage 4 CKD (eGFR 15 to 29 mL/min/1.73m2).

Acetazolamide selectively inhibits luminal membrane carbonic anhydrase IV and cytoplasmic carbonic anhydrase II in the proximal tubule, blocking sodium bicarbonate reabsorption and inducing alkaline diuresis.

The diuretic braking phenomenon describes the progressive reduction in natriuretic response following chronic loop diuretic administration, driven by volume depletion, RAAS and sympathetic activation, and distal tubular epithelial remodeling.

Spot spot urinary sodium assessment after a loop diuretic dose (guideline target spot urine sodium > 50 to 70 mmol/L at 2 hours) serves as a rapid biomarker of diuretic adequacy to guide urgent dose escalation.

Amiloride and triamterene block apical epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) in the cortical collecting duct independently of aldosterone, sparing potassium while causing mild natriuresis and metabolic acidosis.

topics.title: AKI definition, staging and evaluation
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 67-68; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 28; Harrison 22e Ch. 318

mustKnow.fact: KDIGO defines acute kidney injury as an increase in serum creatinine by >= 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours, an increase >= 1.5 times baseline within 7 days, or urine volume < 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours.

KDIGO Stage 3 AKI criteria comprise a 3.0-fold increase in serum creatinine from baseline, serum creatinine >= 4.0 mg/dL with acute rise >= 0.5 mg/dL, initiation of kidney replacement therapy, or anuria for >= 12 hours.

Fractional excretion of sodium (FENa = [UNa x PCr] / [PNa x UCr] x 100) < 1% classically denotes prerenal azotemia, but FENa can be misleadingly elevated above 1% in prerenal states with concomitant diuretic therapy or baseline CKD.

Fractional excretion of urea nitrogen (FEUrea = [UUrea x PCr] / [PUrea x UCr] x 100) < 35% reliably differentiates prerenal azotemia from acute tubular necrosis in patients receiving diuretic therapy.

Urine-to-plasma creatinine ratio > 40, urine osmolality > 500 mOsm/kg, and specific gravity > 1.020 indicate intact tubular concentrating ability in prerenal azotemia, whereas ratios < 20 and isosthenuria (280 to 320 mOsm/kg) indicate acute tubular necrosis.

The furosemide stress test (FST) administers 1.0 mg/kg IV furosemide in loop-diuretic naive patients (1.5 mg/kg in prior users); a urine output < 200 mL within 2 hours predicts progression to severe stage 3 AKI and need for KRT.

Persistent AKI progressing beyond 7 days without recovery is categorized as acute kidney disease (AKD), which transitions to chronic kidney disease if renal functional impairment persists beyond 90 days.

Subclinical AKI represents biomarker-positive (NGAL, KIM-1, TIMP-2 x IGFBP7) tubular damage occurring in the absence of functional changes in serum creatinine or urine output, carrying an increased risk of mortality.

topics.title: Acute tubular necrosis and rhabdomyolysis
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 69; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 29; Harrison 22e Ch. 318

mustKnow.fact: Ischemic acute tubular necrosis selectively injures the S3 segment of the proximal tubule in the outer stripe of the outer medulla and the medullary thick ascending limb due to high metabolic demand and borderline baseline tissue oxygenation.

Loss of proximal tubular epithelial cell polarity with mislocalization of basolateral Na+-K+-ATPase pumps to the apical brush border causes failure of sodium reabsorption and activation of tubuloglomerular feedback vasoconstriction.

Rhabdomyolysis-induced AKI arises from the triad of intrarenal vasoconstriction, direct heme protein proximal tubular cytotoxicity, and intratubular cast formation by myoglobin precipitation with Tamm-Horsfall protein at acid urine pH < 5.6.

In rhabdomyolysis, serum creatine kinase (CK) levels exceeding 5,000 U/L correlate with significant risk of AKI, typically accompanied by severe hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, and early profound hypocalcemia.

Initial management of rhabdomyolysis requires aggressive intravenous volume expansion with isotonic crystalloids targeting a urine output of 200 to 300 mL/h, while urinary alkalinization with sodium bicarbonate is reserved for patients without hypocalcemia when urine pH < 6.5.

Sepsis-associated AKI is primarily driven by microvascular shunting, endothelial dysfunction, glycocalyx degradation, and tubular cellular metabolic reprogramming, rather than global renal hypoperfusion or classic tubular necrosis.

Heme pigment cast nephropathy characteristically exhibits pigmented red-brown granular casts with negative urine dipstick microscopic red blood cells despite strongly positive dipstick orthotolidine blood reaction.

Late hypercalcemia occurs during the diuretic recovery phase of rhabdomyolysis-induced AKI due to mobilization of calcium phosphate complexes previously sequestered within damaged necrotic skeletal muscle tissue.

topics.title: Contrast and drug-induced nephrotoxicity
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 70-71; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 30; Harrison 22e Ch. 319

mustKnow.fact: The PRESERVE trial demonstrated that intravenous sodium bicarbonate is not superior to intravenous isotonic saline, and oral N-acetylcysteine provides no benefit, in preventing contrast-associated acute kidney injury.

Volume prophylaxis with isotonic intravenous saline (1.0 to 1.5 mL/kg/h for 3 to 12 hours before and 6 to 12 hours after iodinated radiocontrast) remains the only proven pharmacological strategy for contrast-associated AKI prevention.

Aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity involves megalin-receptor mediated endocytosis into proximal tubule lysosomes, inducing phospholipidosis and tubular necrosis, classically manifesting as non-oliguric AKI after 7 to 10 days of therapy.

Vancomycin-associated acute kidney injury risk increases significantly with trough levels exceeding 20 mcg/mL or AUC0-24 > 600 mg.h/L, and is markedly potentiated by synergistic tubular toxicity with concomitant piperacillin-tazobactam.

Liposomal amphotericin B significantly reduces nephrotoxicity compared to conventional amphotericin B deoxycholate, which causes intense afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction, proximal tubulopathy, distal RTA, and severe hypokalemia.

Cisplatin induces dose-dependent proximal and distal tubular damage through organic cation transporter 2 (OCT2) uptake and mitochondrial apoptosis, presenting with severe hypomagnesemia and Fanconi-like tubulopathy.

Calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, cyclosporine) cause acute reversible nephrotoxicity via endothelin-mediated afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction, and chronic irreversible nephrotoxicity characterized by arteriolar hyalinosis and striped interstitial fibrosis.

Acyclovir precipitates as needle-shaped birefringent crystals in collecting duct lumens when administered as a rapid intravenous bolus without hydration, inducing acute obstructive intratubular crystal nephropathy.

topics.title: Cardiorenal and hepatorenal syndromes
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 72-73; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 31; Harrison 22e Ch. 320

mustKnow.fact: Type 1 cardiorenal syndrome represents acute decompensated heart failure inducing acute kidney injury, where renal venous congestion (elevated central venous pressure) is the primary hemodynamic determinant of GFR decline.

Type 2 cardiorenal syndrome comprises chronic heart failure causing progressive chronic kidney disease, while Type 3 is acute renocardiac (AKI causing acute heart failure), and Type 4 is chronic renocardiac (CKD causing left ventricular hypertrophy).

Worsening renal function during aggressive decongestive therapy in acute decompensated heart failure is often benign hemoconcentration and does not require diuretic cessation if successful clinical decongestion is being achieved.

Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS-AKI) criteria by the International Club of Cirrhosis require cirrhosis with ascites, diagnosis of AKI by KDIGO criteria, absence of shock, no improvement after 48 hours of diuretic withdrawal and 20% albumin expansion (1 g/kg/day), and no structural kidney disease.

The CONFIRM trial established that terlipressin (continuous IV infusion or 1 to 2 mg boluses every 4 to 6 hours) combined with intravenous albumin significantly improves verified reversal of hepatorenal syndrome.

Norepinephrine infusion (titrated to raise mean arterial pressure by 10 to 15 mmHg) combined with albumin represents an equally effective alternative first-line vasoconstrictor regimen for HRS-AKI in intensive care units.

Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) reduces sinusoidal hypertension and effective arterial underfilling, improving renal perfusion and refractory ascites in selected cirrhotic patients with preserved bilirubin and low MELD score.

Liver transplantation is the definitive curative treatment for hepatorenal syndrome; simultaneous liver-kidney transplantation (SLKT) is indicated if AKI requires dialysis for >= 4 weeks or baseline CKD (eGFR < 30 mL/min/1.73m2) persists.

topics.title: Tropical and community-acquired AKI
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 74; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 32; Harrison 22e Ch. 320

mustKnow.fact: Russell viper (Daboia russelii) bite causes venom-induced consumption coagulopathy (VICC), capillary leak syndrome, acute tubular necrosis, and bilateral renal cortical necrosis due to direct venom metalloproteinases and microvascular thrombosis.

Hump-nosed pit viper (Hypnale hypnale) envenomation is a major cause of venomous AKI and cortical necrosis in Sri Lanka and Southwest India, characteristically causing coagulopathy with normal prothrombin time but prolonged 20-minute whole blood clotting time.

Leptospirosis (Weil disease) produces acute interstitial nephritis and tubular necrosis classically manifesting as hypokalemic, non-oliguric AKI with profound conjunctival suffusion, jaundice, and marked thrombocytopenia.

Falciparum malaria induces severe blackwater fever and AKI through heavy intravascular hemolysis, cytoadherence of parasitized erythrocytes to renal microvasculature, and heme-protein cast nephropathy.

Scrub typhus (Orientia tsutsugamushi) presents with an inoculation eschar, fever, lymphadenopathy, and AKI mediated by systemic endothelial vasculitis, responsive to prompt doxycycline or azithromycin therapy.

Bilateral renal cortical necrosis accounts for up to 5% to 10% of tropical AKI, predominantly triggered by obstetric catastrophes (abruptio placentae, septic abortion) and viperine snakebites, diagnosed by non-enhancing renal cortex with a thin rim of subcapsular enhancement.

Hantavirus infection (hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, HFRS) caused by rodent-borne Dobrava or Puumala viruses presents with fever, thrombocytopenia, marked retroperitoneal edema, and acute oliguric tubulointerstitial nephritis.

Community-acquired diarrheal hemolytic uremic syndrome (STEC-HUS) in children and adults follows Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (O157:H7) infection, manifesting with the triad of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and oliguric AKI.

topics.title: Kidney replacement therapy in AKI
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 75; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 33; Harrison 22e Ch. 321

mustKnow.fact: The STARRT-AKI and AKIKI randomized controlled trials established that an accelerated or early strategy for kidney replacement therapy in critically ill AKI does not reduce 90-day mortality compared with an expectant watch-and-wait strategy.

Absolute emergency indications for initiating kidney replacement therapy in AKI comprise refractory severe hyperkalemia (> 6.5 mmol/L with ECG changes), intractable severe metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.15), refractory pulmonary edema, and overt uremic complications.

Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) is strongly preferred over intermittent hemodialysis in hemodynamically unstable critically ill patients with septic shock, acute liver failure, or acute brain injury with elevated intracranial pressure.

The guideline-recommended target effluent delivery dose for continuous renal replacement therapy in acute kidney injury is 20 to 25 mL/kg/h, which typically requires a prescribed dose of 25 to 30 mL/kg/h to account for interruptions.

Regional citrate anticoagulation (RCA) is recommended as the first-line circuit anticoagulation method for CRRT in patients without contraindications, providing superior circuit filter survival and lower bleeding complications compared with systemic heparin.

Citrate accumulation ('citrate toxicity') during CRRT is diagnosed by a total calcium to ionized calcium ratio > 2.5, worsening metabolic acidosis with an elevated anion gap, and sudden drop in systemic ionized calcium.

Sustained low-efficiency dialysis (SLED) combines the hemodynamic stability of continuous therapies with the operational flexibility and lower consumable cost of intermittent hemodialysis, running blood flows of 150 to 200 mL/min over 6 to 12 hours.

Criteria for attempting discontinuation of KRT in recovering AKI include spontaneous 24-hour urine output > 400 to 500 mL/day without diuretics (or > 1,000 mL/day with diuretics) and spontaneous clearance meeting metabolic demand.

modules.name: Approach to glomerular disease and nephrotic syndrome

topics.title: Approach to glomerular disease and nephrotic syndrome
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 18-20; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 34; Harrison 22e Ch. 322

mustKnow.fact: Nephrotic syndrome is clinically defined by heavy proteinuria (> 3.5 g/24 h per 1.73 m2 or spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio > 3.0 to 3.5 g/g), severe hypoalbuminemia (< 3.0 g/dL), peripheral edema, and hyperlipidemia.

Venous thromboembolism (particularly renal vein thrombosis, DVT, and pulmonary embolism) develops in up to 10% to 30% of nephrotic patients, risk being highest in membranous nephropathy with serum albumin < 2.0 to 2.5 g/dL.

Prophylactic anticoagulation in nephrotic syndrome is guided by bleeding risk and serum albumin, strongly indicated when serum albumin is < 2.0 to 2.5 g/dL with severe proteinuria (> 10 g/day), BMI > 35 kg/m2, or underlying membranous nephropathy.

Hyperlipidemia in nephrotic syndrome features elevated LDL and triglycerides driven by hepatic overproduction of ApoB-100-containing lipoproteins in response to low oncotic pressure and decreased catabolism by lipoprotein lipase.

The underfill hypothesis attributes nephrotic edema to low plasma oncotic pressure triggering secondary renal sodium and water retention via RAAS activation, whereas the overfill hypothesis invokes primary distal tubular ENaC activation by filtered plasmin.

Nephrotic patients exhibit susceptibility to encapsulated bacterial infections (Streptococcus pneumoniae peritonitis and cellulitis) secondary to urinary loss of immunoglobulin IgG and complement factors (factor B, properdin).

Nephritic syndrome is characterized by the sudden onset of gross or microscopic hematuria with dysmorphic red cells and RBC casts, mild-to-moderate non-nephrotic proteinuria, hypertension, oliguria, and elevated serum creatinine.

Glomerular basement membrane charge and size selectivity barrier resides within the fenestrated endothelium with glycocalyx, the trilaminar GBM (rich in heparan sulfate proteoglycans), and the podocyte slit diaphragms spanned by nephrin and podocin.

topics.title: Minimal change disease and FSGS
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 21-22; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 35; Harrison 22e Ch. 322

mustKnow.fact: Minimal change disease (MCD) displays completely normal glomeruli on light microscopy and negative immunofluorescence, with diagnosis established by diffuse, uniform effacement of podocyte foot processes on electron microscopy.

First-line therapy for adult minimal change disease is oral prednisone (1 mg/kg/day, maximum 80 mg/day, or 2 mg/kg alternate days) for a minimum of 4 weeks until complete remission, followed by a slow taper over 6 months.

Frequently relapsing or steroid-dependent adult MCD is treated with oral cyclophosphamide (2 mg/kg/day for 8 to 12 weeks), calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, cyclosporine), or anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody rituximab.

Primary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is mediated by a putative circulating permeability factor (such as soluble urokinase plasminogen activator receptor, suPAR), causing diffuse podocyte injury with sudden nephrotic syndrome.

The Columbia classification categorizes FSGS into five light microscopic histologic variants: collapsing (worst prognosis), tip (best steroid response), cellular, perihilar (typical of secondary adaptive hyperfiltration), and not otherwise specified (NOS).

Secondary non-genetic FSGS results from maladaptive glomerular hyperfiltration in reduced nephron mass (unilateral renal agenesis, reflux nephropathy) or morbid obesity, presenting with non-nephrotic or indolent proteinuria without severe hypoalbuminemia.

APOL1 risk alleles (G1 and G2) inherited homozygously or in compound heterozygosity in individuals of recent African ancestry confer markedly increased susceptibility to hypertensive nephrosclerosis, collapsing FSGS, and HIVAN.

Sparsentan, a dual endothelin A and angiotensin II type 1 receptor antagonist, demonstrated significant reduction in proteinuria compared with irbesartan in patients with primary FSGS in the DUPLEX clinical trial.

topics.title: Membranous nephropathy
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 23; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 36; Harrison 22e Ch. 322

mustKnow.fact: Autoantibodies against the M-type phospholipase A2 receptor (anti-PLA2R, predominantly IgG4 subclass) account for 70% to 80% of primary membranous nephropathy cases, correlating closely with disease activity, remission, and relapse.

Thrombospondin type-1 domain-containing 7A (THSD7A), neural epidermal growth factor-like 1 (NELL-1, frequently malignancy-associated), and exostosin 1 and 2 (EXT1/EXT2, associated with autoimmune disease) represent other specific antigenic targets.

Kidney biopsy in membranous nephropathy demonstrates diffuse glomerular basement membrane thickening on light microscopy, granular capillary loop IgG and C3 on immunofluorescence, and subepithelial electron-dense deposits with intervening spike-and-dome GBM projections.

The MENTOR randomized trial established that B-cell depletion with rituximab (1,000 mg IV on days 1 and 15) is non-inferior to cyclosporine at 12 months and superior in maintaining complete or partial remission through 24 months.

The modified Ponticelli cyclical regimen alternates oral/IV corticosteroids with oral cyclophosphamide monthly for 6 months, reserved for patients with very high-risk disease (rapidly declining eGFR or life-threatening nephrotic complications).

KDIGO guidelines stratify membranous nephropathy into low risk (normal eGFR, proteinuria < 3.5 g/day, anti-PLA2R negative), moderate risk, high risk (proteinuria > 8 g/day or anti-PLA2R > 50 RU/mL), and very high risk.

Secondary membranous nephropathy causes include systemic lupus erythematosus (Class V lupus nephritis), solid organ malignancies (carcinoma of lung, colon, stomach, breast), chronic hepatitis B infection, and drugs (NSAIDs, penicillamine, gold).

Serial monitoring of anti-PLA2R antibody titers allows immunological monitoring: antibody disappearance (immunological remission) precedes clinical reduction in proteinuria (clinical remission) by a median of 3 to 6 months.

topics.title: IgA nephropathy and IgA vasculitis
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 24; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 37; Harrison 22e Ch. 322

mustKnow.fact: IgA nephropathy pathogenesis involves a multi-hit mechanism: hit 1 is elevated galactose-deficient IgA1 (Gd-IgA1); hit 2 is autoantibodies against Gd-IgA1 hinge-region O-glycans; hit 3 is circulating immune complex formation; hit 4 is mesangial deposition and inflammation.

Clinical presentation features recurrent episodes of macroscopic (gross) hematuria coinciding within 24 to 48 hours of upper respiratory or GI infections (synpharyngitic hematuria), contrasting with post-streptococcal GN which occurs after 1 to 3 weeks.

Diagnostic renal biopsy reveals dominant or co-dominant granular mesangial IgA and C3 deposition on immunofluorescence, accompanied by variable mesangial hypercellularity and matrix expansion on light and electron microscopy.

The revised Oxford classification (MEST-C score) independently predicts renal outcome using five histological variables: Mesangial hypercellularity (M0/M1), Endocapillary hypercellularity (E0/E1), Segmental sclerosis (S0/S1), Tubular atrophy/interstitial fibrosis (T0/T1/T2), and Crescents (C0/C1/C2).

Optimized supportive care with maximally tolerated RAAS inhibition (ACE inhibitors or ARBs), SGLT2 inhibitors (DAPA-CKD, EMPA-KIDNEY), and blood pressure control (< 120 mmHg systolic) represents foundational first-line therapy.

Targeted-release formulation of oral budesonide (Nefecon, 16 mg once daily for 9 months) in the NefIgArd trial significantly reduced proteinuria and slowed eGFR loss by delivering drug locally to ileal Peyer patches.

The PROTECT trial demonstrated that sparsentan (dual endothelin A and angiotensin II receptor antagonist, 400 mg daily) significantly achieved greater proteinuria reduction compared to active control irbesartan in high-risk IgA nephropathy.

IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura) in adults combines IgA nephropathy histology with systemic small-vessel leukocytoclastic vasculitis manifesting as non-thrombocytopenic palpable purpura, arthralgias, and colicky gastrointestinal pain.

topics.title: Infection-related glomerulonephritis
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 25; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 38; Harrison 22e Ch. 322

mustKnow.fact: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) follows Group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus pharyngeal infection by a latent period of 1 to 2 weeks, or impetigo and pyoderma by a latent period of 3 to 6 weeks.

Cationic streptococcal nephritogenic antigens, particularly nephritis-associated plasmin receptor (NAPlr) and streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin B (SPEB), deposit in glomeruli and activate complement via the alternative pathway.

Biopsy in PSGN characteristically shows diffuse endocapillary proliferative and exudative glomerulonephritis packed with neutrophils, 'starry sky' capillary wall C3 deposits, and large subepithelial humps on electron microscopy.

Serum complement C3 is markedly depressed in > 90% of PSGN cases at presentation, with normalization of serum C3 levels expected within 6 to 8 weeks; persistence beyond 8 to 12 weeks mandates consideration of C3 glomerulopathy or MPGN.

Anti-streptolysin O (ASO) titers rise following pharyngeal streptococcal infection, whereas anti-DNase B and anti-hyaluronidase titers are markedly more sensitive and reliable following cutaneous impetigo.

Staphylococcal infection-associated glomerulonephritis (often methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, MRSA) typically affects older diabetics with active ongoing visceral abscesses, osteomyelitis, or endocarditis, characteristically showing dominant mesangial and capillary IgA deposition.

Infective endocarditis-associated glomerulonephritis manifests with hypocomplementemia (depressed C3 and C4), circulating ANCA positivity (often PR3 or MPO) in up to 20% to 30%, and a focal necrotizing or crescentic GN histology.

Shunt nephritis arises from chronic indolent colonization of ventriculoatrial CSF shunts by Propionibacterium acnes or Staphylococcus epidermidis, presenting with MPGN-like histology and resolving completely upon shunt removal.

topics.title: MPGN and C3 glomerulopathy
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 26; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 39; Harrison 22e Ch. 322

mustKnow.fact: Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) is a light microscopic histological pattern characterized by mesangial hypercellularity, endocapillary proliferation, and glomerular capillary wall remodeling showing duplication and 'tram-track' double contours.

The modern immunofluorescence-based classification divides MPGN into immune-complex mediated MPGN (significant immunoglobulin and complement staining) versus complement-mediated MPGN (C3 dominant staining with absent or trace immunoglobulins).

C3 glomerulopathy (C3G) is defined by immunofluorescence showing C3 intensity at least two orders of magnitude greater than any immunoglobulin staining (C3 intensity >= 2+ on a 0-to-3+ scale with negative or trace Ig).

Dense deposit disease (DDD) is distinguished from C3 glomerulonephritis (C3GN) by electron microscopy showing highly electron-dense, continuous ribbon-like osmiophilic transformation within the lamina densa of the glomerular basement membrane.

C3 nephritic factor (C3NeF) is an IgG autoantibody directed against the alternative complement pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb), binding to and stabilizing the convertase against decay to produce continuous, uncontrolled fluid-phase C3 consumption.

Immune complex-mediated MPGN in adults requires rigorous clinical exclusion of chronic viral hepatitis (hepatitis C with or without type II mixed cryoglobulinemia), monoclonal gammopathy (MGRS), and systemic autoimmune diseases.

Acquired partial lipodystrophy (Barraquer-Simons syndrome) and bilateral retinal drusen are strong clinical extrarenal phenotypic associations specifically seen in patients with dense deposit disease.

Iptacopan, an oral small-molecule factor B inhibitor targeting the alternative complement pathway, demonstrated significant reduction in proteinuria in patients with C3 glomerulopathy in the pivotal APPEAR-C3G clinical trial.

topics.title: RPGN and ANCA-associated vasculitis
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 27-28; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 40; Harrison 22e Ch. 323

mustKnow.fact: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) is a clinical syndrome of rapid decline in GFR (> 50% loss over weeks to months) accompanied by active nephritic urine sediment and extensive glomerular crescent formation involving > 50% of glomeruli.

Pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis accounts for 80% of RPGN in older adults, characterized on biopsy by segmental necrosis, cellular crescents, and lack of significant immunoglobulin or complement deposition on immunofluorescence.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) is predominantly associated with cytoplasmic ANCA (c-ANCA) directed against proteinase 3 (PR3-ANCA), whereas microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) is associated with perinuclear ANCA (p-ANCA) directed against myeloperoxidase (MPO-ANCA).

The RAVE trial established that rituximab (375 mg/m2 weekly for 4 weeks) is non-inferior to oral cyclophosphamide for remission induction in severe ANCA-associated vasculitis and superior in patients presenting with relapsing disease.

The PEXIVAS trial demonstrated that routine therapeutic plasma exchange (PEX) does not reduce the long-term incidence of end-stage kidney disease or all-cause mortality in patients with severe ANCA-associated vasculitis.

Avacopan, an oral selective complement C5a receptor 1 (C5aR1) antagonist evaluated in the ADVOCATE trial, is effective for remission induction and allows complete elimination of high-dose systemic corticosteroid exposure.

The Berden histological classification of ANCA glomerulonephritis stratifies biopsy prognosis into four distinct classes: focal (>= 50% normal glomeruli, best prognosis), crescentic (>= 50% cellular crescents), mixed, and sclerotic (>= 50% globally sclerotic, worst prognosis).

Maintenance therapy with rituximab (500 mg IV every 6 months for at least 2 years) is superior to daily oral azathioprine in preventing clinical relapses in ANCA-associated vasculitis according to the MAINRITSAN trial.

topics.title: Anti-GBM disease
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 29; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 41; Harrison 22e Ch. 323

mustKnow.fact: Anti-GBM disease is caused by circulating autoantibodies directed specifically against the non-collagenous domain 1 (NC1) of the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen [alpha3(IV)NC1], encoded by the COL4A3 gene.
Goodpasture syndrome represents the classic pulmonary-renal syndrome triad of rapidly progressive crescentic glomerulonephritis, alveolar pulmonary hemorrhage, and circulating anti-GBM antibodies.
Diagnostic renal biopsy demonstrates bright, continuous, ribbon-like linear IgG staining along glomerular capillary walls on direct immunofluorescence examination.

First-line remission therapy requires urgent initiation of daily therapeutic plasma exchange (4-liter exchanges with 5% albumin replacement for 14 days or until anti-GBM antibodies become undetectable) combined with oral cyclophosphamide and pulse methylprednisolone.

Patients presenting with dialysis-dependent renal failure (serum creatinine > 5.7 mg/dL or 500 mcmol/L) and 100% cellular crescents on biopsy have virtually zero renal recovery potential; aggressive immunosuppression is withheld unless active pulmonary hemorrhage is present.

Up to 30% of patients with anti-GBM disease have co-existing circulating ANCA antibodies (most commonly MPO-ANCA, 'double-positive' disease); these patients behave like anti-GBM acutely but exhibit a propensity for late ANCA vasculitis relapses.
Strong genetic susceptibility is linked to human leukocyte antigen class II alleles HLA-DRB1*1501 and HLA-DRB1*1502, whereas HLA-DRB1*01 and HLA-DRB1*07 confer dominant disease resistance.

Renal transplantation can be safely performed only after circulating anti-GBM antibodies have remained continuously undetectable by sensitive ELISA for at least 6 months, preventing catastrophic recurrent allograft crescentic destruction.

topics.title: Lupus nephritis
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 30; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 42; Harrison 22e Ch. 324

mustKnow.fact: The 2003 ISN/RPS classification categorizes lupus nephritis into six classes: Class I (minimal mesangial), Class II (mesangial proliferative), Class III (focal, < 50% glomeruli), Class IV (diffuse, >= 50% glomeruli), Class V (membranous), and Class VI (advanced sclerosing, >= 90% sclerosed).

Class IV diffuse lupus nephritis is subdivided into IV-S (segmental) and IV-G (global), displaying active wire-loop lesions (massive subendothelial immune deposits), hyaline thrombi, and endocapillary proliferation.

Diagnostic renal biopsy reveals a 'full house' immunofluorescence pattern, showing intense simultaneous staining for all three immunoglobulin classes (IgG, IgA, IgM) and both complement components (C3, C1q).

First-line induction therapy for active Class III or IV lupus nephritis consists of pulse methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisone combined with either mycophenolate mofetil (MMF 2 to 3 g/day) or low-dose intravenous cyclophosphamide (Euro-Lupus regimen, 500 mg every 2 weeks for 6 doses).

The BLISS-LN trial demonstrated that adding belimumab (anti-BAFF/BLyS monoclonal antibody) to standard therapy significantly increases primary efficacy renal response and reduces renal flares and eGFR decline.

The AURINIA trial established that triple immunosuppressive therapy incorporating voclosporin (a novel calcineurin inhibitor) with MMF and low-dose steroids significantly doubles complete renal response rates in active lupus nephritis.

Hydroxychloroquine is recommended for all patients with lupus nephritis unless contraindicated, significantly reducing renal flare rates, chronic kidney damage accrual, thrombotic events, and all-cause mortality.

National Institutes of Health (NIH) activity index (scored 0 to 24, including endocapillary hypercellularity, karyorrhexis, crescents double-weighted) and chronicity index (scored 0 to 12, including glomerulosclerosis, interstitial fibrosis) guide treatment intensity and reversibility.

topics.title: Paraprotein-related kidney disease and amyloidosis
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 31-32; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 43; Harrison 22e Ch. 325

mustKnow.fact: Myeloma cast nephropathy (light chain cast nephropathy) is the most common cause of severe AKI in multiple myeloma, caused by monoclonal free light chains (kappa or lambda) coprecipitating with Tamm-Horsfall mucoprotein in distal tubules into fractured, giant-cell-surrounded casts.

AL amyloidosis is caused by monoclonal immunoglobulin light chain (lambda in 75% to 80%) misfolding into insoluble 7.5 to 10 nm non-branching antiparallel beta-pleated sheet fibrils, exhibiting apple-green birefringence under polarized light after Congo red staining.

Monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance (MGRS) defines a clonal B-cell or plasma cell proliferative disorder that does not meet hematologic criteria for overt myeloma or lymphoma but produces a nephrotoxic monoclonal immunoglobulin causing kidney disease.

Light chain deposition disease (LCDD, predominantly kappa light chains in 80%) features nodular glomerulosclerosis resembling diabetic nephropathy on light microscopy, with continuous non-fibrillar linear kappa light chain deposition along glomerular and tubular basement membranes.

The ANDROMEDA trial established that subcutaneous daratumumab (anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody) combined with bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone (D-VCd) produces superior hematologic and organ response in newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis.

AA amyloidosis develops secondary to chronic persistent inflammation (rheumatoid arthritis, bronchiectasis, familial Mediterranean fever) mediated by serum amyloid A (SAA) protein cleavage and deposition, showing loss of Congo red affinity following potassium permanganate pretreatment.

Serum free light chain (sFLC) ratio (normal kappa/lambda ratio 0.26 to 1.65, renal reference range 0.37 to 3.10 in CKD) with involved FLC > 1,500 mg/L (or 100 mg/dL) correlates directly with light chain cast nephropathy risk.

C3 glomerulopathy with monoclonal gammopathy is an increasingly recognized form of MGRS in older adults, where monoclonal paraproteins act as autoantibodies activating the alternative complement pathway (e.g., monoclonal C3NeF).

topics.title: Diabetic kidney disease
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 33; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 44; Harrison 22e Ch. 326

mustKnow.fact: Pathognomonic histological lesion of diabetic nephropathy is nodular intercapillary glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules), accompanied by diffuse GBM thickening, mesangial expansion, capsular drops, and arteriolar hyalinosis.

SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin) reduce glomerular hyperfiltration via restoring tubuloglomerular feedback, demonstrating consistent 30% to 40% reduction in CKD progression, kidney failure, and cardiovascular death across CREDENCE, DAPA-CKD, and EMPA-KIDNEY trials.

Finerenone, a non-steroidal selective mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist evaluated in the FIDELIO-DKD and FIGARO-DKD trials, significantly reduces kidney disease progression and cardiovascular events on top of maximally tolerated ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy.

The FLOW trial demonstrated that the subcutaneous GLP-1 receptor agonist semaglutide (1.0 mg weekly) significantly reduces major kidney disease events and cardiovascular mortality in patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease.

Hyperfiltration phase of diabetic nephropathy is characterized by an early elevation in measured GFR (often 140 to 180 mL/min/1.73m2) driven by hyperglycemia-mediated proximal SGLT2 sodium and glucose hyper-reabsorption, suppressing distal macula densa sodium delivery.

Normoalbuminuric diabetic kidney disease (NADKD) accounts for 20% to 40% of declining GFR in diabetic patients, characterized on biopsy by predominant interstitial fibrosis and arteriolar sclerosis rather than classical nodular mesangial expansion.
Target blood pressure in diabetic kidney disease with albuminuria is < 120 mmHg systolic using standardized automated office BP measurement, as recommended by KDIGO 2023 guidelines.

Dual RAAS blockade combining an ACE inhibitor with an ARB or direct renin inhibitor (aliskiren) is strictly contraindicated in diabetic kidney disease due to clinical trial evidence (ONTARGET, VA NEPHRON-D, ALTITUDE) demonstrating increased hyperkalemia, acute kidney injury, and stroke without renal benefit.

modules.name: Thrombotic microangiopathy and hypertensive kidney disease

topics.title: Thrombotic microangiopathy and hypertensive kidney disease
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 34; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 45; Harrison 22e Ch. 327

mustKnow.fact: Thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) is defined by the pathological triad of microvascular endothelial injury, microvascular thrombosis, and erythrocyte fragmentation producing microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA with schistocytes) and thrombocytopenia.

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) is caused by severe deficiency of the von Willebrand factor-cleaving protease ADAMTS13 (activity < 10%), mediated by acquired autoantibodies or congenital mutations (Upshaw-Schulman syndrome).

Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) is driven by uncontrolled dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway, caused by loss-of-function mutations in regulatory proteins (CFH, CFI, CD46/MCP) or gain-of-function mutations in C3 or CFB.

Eculizumab and ravulizumab are recombinant humanized monoclonal antibodies that bind complement protein C5, blocking cleavage into C5a and terminal membrane attack complex (C5b-9) assembly, representing first-line targeted therapy for aHUS.

Caplacizumab is an anti-von Willebrand factor humanized single-variable-domain antibody (nanobody) that inhibits the interaction between vWF multimer A1 domains and platelet glycoprotein Ib-IX-V, accelerating platelet count recovery in acute TTP.

Malignant nephrosclerosis is characterized histopathologically by hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis ('onion-skin' intimal thickening) and fibrinoid necrosis of afferent arterioles and glomerular tufts, presenting with acute severe hypertensive encephalopathy and AKI.

Benign hypertensive nephrosclerosis features hyaline arteriolosclerosis, medial hypertrophy, subcapsular cortical scarring with a finely granular kidney surface, and ischemic wrinkling of the glomerular basement membrane.

Scleroderma renal crisis (SRC) manifests with acute onset oliguric AKI, accelerated hypertension, and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, where urgent initiation of ACE inhibitors (captopril) is life-saving, whereas systemic corticosteroids increase SRC risk.

sections.name: Tubulointerstitial, cystic and inherited kidney disease

topics.title: Acute and chronic interstitial nephritis
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 35-36; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 46; Harrison 22e Ch. 328

mustKnow.fact: Drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) is most frequently caused by proton pump inhibitors (omeprazole, pantoprazole), beta-lactam antibiotics, fluoroquinolones, sulfonamides, and NSAIDs.

The classic allergic triad of fever, maculopapular rash, and peripheral eosinophilia is present in fewer than 10% of patients with drug-induced AIN, making kidney biopsy the gold standard for definitive diagnosis.

Histopathological hallmarks of acute interstitial nephritis comprise interstitial edema, diffuse mononuclear cell infiltration (T lymphocytes and macrophages), eosinophils, and tubulitis with lymphocytes invading tubular basement membranes.

Early oral corticosteroid therapy (prednisone 1 mg/kg/day for 2 to 3 weeks followed by a 4- to 6-week taper) initiated within 7 to 14 days of culprit drug withdrawal significantly enhances renal recovery and reduces irreversible interstitial fibrosis.

NSAID-induced AIN characteristically differs by presenting with heavy nephrotic-range proteinuria and podocyte foot process effacement resembling minimal change disease alongside interstitial inflammatory infiltration.

IgG4-related tubulointerstitial nephritis demonstrates dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate rich in IgG4-positive plasma cells (> 10 per high-power field, IgG4/IgG ratio > 40%), storiform interstitial fibrosis, and elevated serum IgG4 levels.

Tubulointerstitial nephritis and uveitis (TINU) syndrome predominantly affects young females, presenting with bilateral anterior uveitis, elevated urinary beta-2 microglobulin, and acute tubulointerstitial nephritis responding well to steroids.

Chronic aristolochic acid nephropathy (Balkan endemic nephropathy and Chinese herb nephropathy) causes profound, acellular, hypocellular cortical interstitial fibrosis with severe tubular atrophy and marked predisposition to upper urinary tract urothelial carcinoma.

topics.title: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 37; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 47; Harrison 22e Ch. 329

mustKnow.fact: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is caused by mutations in PKD1 (encoding polycystin-1, chromosome 16p13.3, accounting for 78% of cases, median ESKD age 58 years) or PKD2 (polycystin-2, chromosome 4q21, 15% of cases, median ESKD age 79 years).

Ravine ultrasound diagnostic criteria for at-risk individuals aged 15 to 39 years require at least 3 unilateral or bilateral kidney cysts; for ages 40 to 59 years, at least 2 cysts in each kidney; and for age >= 60 years, at least 4 cysts in each kidney.

The TEMPO 3:4 and REPRISE trials established that the oral selective vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist tolvaptan significantly slows total kidney volume (TKV) growth and eGFR decline in rapidly progressing ADPKD.

The Mayo Imaging Classification stratifies ADPKD progression risk based on height-adjusted total kidney volume (HtTKV) and age into Class 1A through 1E, where Classes 1C, 1D, and 1E define rapid progressors eligible for tolvaptan.

Intracranial saccular berry aneurysms occur in 9% to 12% of ADPKD patients (up to 20% with family history of intracranial aneurysm or subarachnoid hemorrhage), indicating magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) screening.

Hepatic cysts are the most common extrarenal manifestation of ADPKD (affecting > 80% by age 35), being more extensive in females and multiparous women due to estrogen exposure, but rarely compromising hepatic synthetic function.

Infected renal cysts in ADPKD present with localized flank pain, fever, and leukocytosis, requiring prolonged lipophilic antibiotic therapy (fluoroquinolones, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) that effectively penetrates cyst walls.

The HALT-PKD trial showed that rigorous blood pressure control (95/60 to 110/75 mmHg) in young ADPKD patients with preserved GFR slowed the rate of total kidney volume increase without significant effect on eGFR decline.

modules.name: Alport syndrome and thin basement membrane disease

topics.title: Alport syndrome and thin basement membrane disease
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 38; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 48; Harrison 22e Ch. 329

mustKnow.fact: Alport syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in COL4A5 on chromosome Xq22.3 in 85% of cases (X-linked Alport syndrome), or bi-allelic variants in autosomal COL4A3 or COL4A4 on chromosome 2q36 (autosomal recessive Alport syndrome).
Pathognomonic electron microscopic finding in Alport syndrome is irregular thinning, thickening, splitting, and 'basket-weave' lamellation of the glomerular basement membrane lamina densa.

Sensorineural hearing loss in Alport syndrome is progressive, bilateral, symmetrical, and initially affects high frequencies (2,000 to 8,000 Hz), sparing conversational frequencies in early childhood.

Pathognomonic ocular signs in Alport syndrome include anterior lenticonus (conical protrusion of the anterior lens capsule into the anterior chamber in 25% of cases) and central dot-and-fleck retinopathy.

Early initiation of ACE inhibitors (ramipril, enalapril) or ARBs significantly delays onset of end-stage kidney disease and extends life expectancy by decades in both males and females with Alport syndrome.

Thin basement membrane nephropathy (benign familial hematuria) is caused by heterozygous carrier mutations in COL4A3 or COL4A4, displaying diffuse thinning of the GBM (< 200 to 250 nm) with normal lamellation and lifelong preserved renal function.

Following kidney transplantation in Alport syndrome, approximately 3% to 5% of patients develop de novo anti-GBM crescentic glomerulonephritis directed against the donor allograft's alpha-5 or alpha-3 type IV collagen chains.

Diffuse leiomyomatosis of the esophagus, tracheobronchial tree, and female genitalia occurs in a subset of Alport syndrome cases caused by contiguous gene deletions spanning the adjacent COL4A5 and COL4A6 genes.

topics.title: Inherited tubulopathies
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 39; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 49; Harrison 22e Ch. 330

mustKnow.fact: Bartter syndrome is an autosomal recessive salt-wasting tubulopathy of the thick ascending limb caused by mutations in NKCC2 (Type 1, SLC12A1), ROMK (Type 2, KCNJ1), CLC-Kb (Type 3, CLCNKB), or barttin (Type 4, BSND with sensorineural deafness).
Bartter syndrome manifests with hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, hyperreninemic hyperaldosteronism, normal-to-low blood pressure, hypercalciuria, and early medullary nephrocalcinosis.

Gitelman syndrome is an autosomal recessive tubulopathy of the distal convoluted tubule caused by loss-of-function mutations in the thiazide-sensitive NaCl cotransporter NCC (SLC12A3), manifesting in adolescence or adulthood.

Gitelman syndrome is clinically distinguished from Bartter syndrome by the presence of prominent hypocalciuria (calcium-to-creatinine ratio < 0.20 mg/mg or < 0.05 mmol/mmol) and severe hypomagnesemia without nephrocalcinosis.

Liddle syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by gain-of-function mutations in the PY motif of beta or gamma subunits of ENaC (SCNN1B, SCNN1G), disrupting NEDD4-2 ubiquitin ligase-mediated channel internalization.

Liddle syndrome presents with early severe hypertension, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, suppressed plasma renin activity, and undetectable serum aldosterone (pseudoaldosteronism), which responds selectively to amiloride or triamterene.

Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1 (PHA1) features renal salt wasting, hyperkalemic metabolic acidosis, and elevated renin and aldosterone; autosomal dominant PHA1 is caused by mineralocorticoid receptor (NR3C2) mutations, while autosomal recessive PHA1 is caused by loss-of-function ENaC mutations.

Gordon syndrome (pseudohypoaldosteronism type 2, familial hyperkalemic hypertension) is caused by mutations in WNK1, WNK4, CUL3, or KLHL3, leading to constitutive activation of the thiazide-sensitive NCC cotransporter and responding rapidly to low-dose thiazides.

modules.name: Other genetic and congenital kidney disorders

topics.title: Other genetic and congenital kidney disorders
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 40; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 50; Harrison 22e Ch. 331

mustKnow.fact: Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD) is caused by mutations in PKHD1 on chromosome 6p12 (encoding fibrocystin/polyductin), characterized by bilateral symmetrically enlarged echogenic kidneys with fusiform collecting duct ectasia and congenital hepatic fibrosis.

Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease (ADTKD) is caused by mutations in UMOD (uromodulin), MUC1 (mucin-1), HNF1B, or REN (renin), characterized by bland urine sediment, medullary cysts in a minority, progressive CKD, and early severe hyperuricemia with gout.

Nephronophthisis (NPHP) is an autosomal recessive ciliopathy and the leading monogenic cause of end-stage kidney disease in children and adolescents, caused most commonly by homozygous NPHP1 full-gene deletions.

Fabry disease is an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of alpha-galactosidase A (GLA gene), leading to cellular accumulation of globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) and globotriaosylsphingosine (lyso-Gb3) within podocytes, vascular endothelium, and cardiomyocytes.

Biopsy in Fabry disease displays characteristic zebra bodies (concentric whorled laminated myelin figures) within podocyte cytoplasm on electron microscopy, treated with recombinant enzyme replacement therapy (agalsidase beta) or the chaperone migalastat.

Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC1 hamartin, TSC2 tuberin) causes multiple bilateral renal angiomyolipomas, renal cysts, and predisposition to renal cell carcinoma, treatable with oral mTOR inhibitors (everolimus) when angiomyolipomas exceed 3 to 4 cm.

Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease is an autosomal dominant syndrome predisposing to bilateral clear cell renal cell carcinomas and multiple pancreatic/renal cysts due to failure of ubiquitin-mediated hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF-1alpha and HIF-2alpha) degradation.

HNF1B-associated disease (renal cysts and diabetes syndrome, RCAD) features renal dysplasia, hypoplastic glomerulocystic kidneys, maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY5), hypomagnesemia, and hyperuricemia.

topics.title: Nephrolithiasis and nephrocalcinosis
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 41-42; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 51; Harrison 22e Ch. 332

mustKnow.fact: Calcium stones account for approximately 75% to 80% of all nephrolithiasis cases, most commonly composed of calcium oxalate (monohydrate whewellite or dihydrate weddellite) and calcium phosphate (apatite or brushite).

Idiopathic hypercalciuria (24-hour urine calcium > 250 mg in women, > 300 mg in men, or > 4 mg/kg/day) is the most prevalent metabolic risk factor for calcium nephrolithiasis, managed with dietary sodium restriction (< 2 g/day) and thiazide diuretics.

Dietary calcium restriction paradoxically increases calcium oxalate stone formation by enhancing uncomplexed free oxalate absorption in the gut; patients are advised to maintain normal dietary calcium intake (1,000 to 1,200 mg/day) taken with meals.

Uric acid stones form exclusively in persistently acidic urine (urine pH < 5.5) where insoluble un-ionized uric acid predominates, appearing radiolucent on conventional plain radiography but readily detectable on non-contrast CT (200 to 400 Hounsfield units).

Therapeutic urinary alkalinization with potassium citrate (targeting a urine pH of 6.5 to 7.0) is the cornerstone of uric acid stone chemolysis and prevention, while allopurinol or febuxostat is added if hyperuricosuria or hyperuricemia persists.

Struvite stones (infection stones, magnesium ammonium phosphate and carbonate apatite) form in alkaline urine (pH > 7.2) infected by urease-producing organisms (Proteus mirabilis, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas), producing branched staghorn calculi.

Cystinuria is an autosomal recessive defect in the dibasic amino acid transporter SLC3A1 (rBAT) or SLC7A9, presenting in young patients with pathognomonic flat hexagonal crystals in acidic urine, positive sodium cyanide-nitroprusside test, and radiopaque ground-glass stones.

Medullary sponge kidney is a congenital non-inherited malformation characterized by cystic dilatation of the collecting ducts in one or more renal pyramids, strongly predisposing to recurrent nephrolithiasis, distal RTA, and medullary nephrocalcinosis.

topics.title: Obstructive uropathy
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 43; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 52; Harrison 22e Ch. 333

mustKnow.fact: Acute bilateral urinary tract obstruction triggers a triphasic hemodynamic response: an initial brief rise in renal blood flow and intratubular pressure (first 1 to 2 hours), followed by progressive renal vasoconstriction with falling blood flow and high pressure (up to 24 hours), and finally persistent vasoconstriction with declining intratubular pressure.

Renal ultrasound is the initial imaging modality of choice to evaluate obstructive uropathy, but false negatives (hydronephrosis absent) occur in early acute obstruction (< 24 to 48 hours), severe retroperitoneal fibrosis, retroperitoneal tumor encasement, or hypovolemia.

Post-obstructive diuresis (POD) is defined as severe urine output exceeding 200 mL/h for at least 2 consecutive hours or > 3 to 4 liters/day following relief of bilateral obstruction or solitary functioning kidney obstruction.

Pathologic post-obstructive diuresis is characterized by inappropriate renal tubular sodium wasting and impaired water reabsorption driven by medullary gradient washout, downregulation of tubular aquaporins (AQP2, AQP3) and NKCC2, and unresponsiveness to vasopressin.

Management of post-obstructive diuresis requires replacement of urinary water and electrolyte losses using 0.45% saline with potassium, replacing approximately 50% to 75% of hourly urinary output to avoid perpetuating iatrogenic volume-expanded diuresis.

Retroperitoneal fibrosis (Ormond disease) causes medial deviation of the middle third of both ureters with extrinsic hydronephrosis, being idiopathic in over two-thirds of cases and frequently representing a manifestation of IgG4-related disease.

Chronic uncorrected urinary tract obstruction induces progressive tubulointerstitial fibrosis, tubular epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta) upregulation, and irreversible nephron loss.

Renal tubular acidosis associated with obstructive uropathy characteristically presents as a hyperkalemic, normal anion gap metabolic acidosis (Type 4 RTA phenotype) caused by collecting duct resistance to aldosterone and impaired proton secretion.

topics.title: Urinary tract infection and pyelonephritis
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 44; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 53; Harrison 22e Ch. 334

mustKnow.fact: Uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) accounts for 75% to 85% of community-acquired uncomplicated urinary tract infections, expressing type 1 fimbriae (binding uroplakin) and P fimbriae (Pap, binding digalactoside receptors in renal pelvis) that mediate tissue invasion.

Acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis in outpatients is treated with oral fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 7 days) if local resistance is < 10%, or oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 14 days following an initial IV ceftriaxone dose.

Asymptomatic bacteriuria (>= 10^5 CFU/mL of identical organism in two consecutive clean-catch voids without symptoms) requires antibiotic treatment ONLY in pregnant individuals and patients undergoing invasive urological procedures breaching the mucosa.

Emphysematous pyelonephritis is a life-threatening necrotizing gas-forming renal infection occurring almost exclusively in patients with diabetes mellitus, caused by glucose fermentation by E. coli or Klebsiella pneumoniae.

Huang and Tseng CT classification stratifies emphysematous pyelonephritis into Class 1 (gas in collecting system only), Class 2 (gas in renal parenchyma without extension), Class 3A/3B (extension into perinephric or pararenal space), and Class 4 (bilateral or solitary kidney).

Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (XPN) is an uncommon chronic destructive granulomatous infection triggered by chronic staghorn calculus obstruction, characterized histologically by lipid-laden foamy macrophages (xanthoma cells) that can mimic renal cell carcinoma.

Renal papillary necrosis manifests with acute flank pain, gross hematuria, and sloughed papillae causing ureteric colic, classic etiologic risk factors remembered by the mnemonic POSTCARDS (pyelonephritis, obstruction, sickle cell disease, tuberculosis, cirrhosis, analgesics, renal transplant, diabetes, systemic vasculitis).
Renal tuberculosis produces sterile pyuria with persistent microscopic hematuria and acid urine; imaging demonstrates infundibular strictures, calyceal amputation, and 'putty kidney' calcification.

topics.title: CKD staging and progression
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 45-46; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 54; Harrison 22e Ch. 335

mustKnow.fact: KDIGO defines chronic kidney disease as abnormalities of kidney structure or function persisting for > 3 months, classified into GFR categories G1 (>= 90 mL/min/1.73m2), G2 (60 to 89), G3a (45 to 59), G3b (30 to 44), G4 (15 to 29), and G5 (< 15 or dialysis).

The KDIGO heat map integrates GFR stages (G1 to G5) with albuminuria stages (A1 < 30 mg/g, A2 30 to 300 mg/g, A3 > 300 mg/g) to stratify risks of CKD progression, cardiovascular mortality, and acute kidney injury.
The 4-variable Kidney Failure Risk Equation (KFRE) calculates the 2-year and 5-year risk of developing end-stage kidney disease using age, sex, eGFR, and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR).

Brenner's hyperfiltration hypothesis posits that initial nephron loss induces compensatory hemodynamic adaptation with afferent arteriolar vasodilation and single-nephron GFR elevation, which drives progressive glomerulosclerosis independent of original etiology.
Dietary sodium restriction to < 2.0 g/day (< 5 g sodium chloride per day) lowers systolic blood pressure, potentiates the antiproteinuric efficacy of RAAS inhibitors, and slows CKD progression.

Metformin therapy must be dose-reduced to maximum 1,000 mg/day when eGFR is 30 to 44 mL/min/1.73m2 and must be completely discontinued when eGFR falls below 30 mL/min/1.73m2 to prevent lactic acidosis.

Guideline-directed oral sodium bicarbonate supplementation targeting serum bicarbonate levels between 22 and 26 mmol/L slows the rate of eGFR decline and improves muscle mass in metabolic acidosis of CKD.

Referral to specialized nephrology multidisciplinary care is strongly recommended when eGFR falls below 30 mL/min/1.73m2 (Stage 4 CKD) or when the 2-year predicted risk of kidney failure by KFRE exceeds 10% to 20%.

topics.title: CKD mineral and bone disorder
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 47; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 55; Harrison 22e Ch. 336

mustKnow.fact: CKD mineral and bone disorder (CKD-MBD) comprises a systemic syndrome manifesting by one or a combination of: laboratory abnormalities of calcium, phosphorus, PTH, or vitamin D; abnormalities in bone turnover, mineralization, or volume; and vascular or soft tissue calcification.

Pathogenesis of secondary hyperparathyroidism begins early in CKD with renal phosphate retention and rising osteocyte FGF23 secretion, which suppresses renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase (CYP27B1) causing calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) deficiency.

KDIGO guidelines suggest maintaining serum intact parathyroid hormone (iPTH) levels in end-stage kidney disease (CKD G5D) in the range of approximately 2 to 9 times the upper normal limit of the assay (typically 130 to 600 pg/mL).

Non-calcium-based phosphate binders (sevelamer carbonate, lanthanum carbonate, sucroferric oxyhydroxide) avoid positive calcium balance and reduce progression of coronary artery and aortic calcification compared with calcium acetate or carbonate.

Calcimimetics (oral cinacalcet, intravenous etelcalcetide) allosterically activate the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) on parathyroid chief cells, suppressing PTH secretion while simultaneously lowering both serum calcium and phosphorus.

Adynamic bone disease is a low-turnover bone disorder characterized histologically by markedly reduced osteoblast and osteoclast activity and low bone formation rate, associated with oversuppression of PTH (iPTH < 100 pg/mL) and increased fracture risk.

Calciphylaxis (calcific uremic arteriolopathy) is a devastating syndrome of small-vessel medial arteriolar calcification, endovascular fibrosis, and microthrombosis causing painful ischemic subcutaneous violaceous plaques and non-healing necrotic ulcers.

Medical management of calciphylaxis incorporates intravenous sodium thiosulfate (25 g infused post-dialysis three times weekly), aggressive wound care, discontinuation of calcium binders and vitamin D analogues, and lowering calcium-phosphorus product.

topics.title: Anaemia of CKD
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 48; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 56; Harrison 22e Ch. 337

mustKnow.fact: The primary etiology of anemia in chronic kidney disease is relative erythropoietin (EPO) deficiency caused by loss of peritubular interstitial fibroblastic renal erythropoietin-producing (REP) cells.

Functional iron deficiency in CKD is mediated by chronic inflammation inducing hepatic overproduction of hepcidin, which internalizes and degrades the iron exporter ferroportin on enterocytes and macrophages, trapping iron within storage pools.

KDIGO defines iron deficiency in CKD as transferrin saturation (TSAT) <= 30% and serum ferritin <= 500 ng/mL, requiring iron supplementation before or alongside erythropoiesis-stimulating agent initiation.
