The CHOIR, CREATE, and TREAT landmark clinical trials established that targeting hemoglobin to normal levels (> 13 g/dL) using high-dose ESAs increases risks of stroke, cardiovascular events, venous thromboembolism, and vascular access thrombosis without improving survival.

Current clinical practice guidelines recommend initiating ESA therapy (epoetin alfa, darbepoetin alfa, methoxy polyethylene glycol-epoetin beta) only when hemoglobin is < 10 g/dL, maintaining hemoglobin between 10.0 and 11.5 g/dL and strictly avoiding levels > 11.5 to 12.0 g/dL.

Hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors (HIF-PHIs: roxadustat, vadadustat, daprodustat) are oral agents that stabilize HIF-alpha subunits, stimulating endogenous erythropoietin production, enhancing iron absorption, and suppressing circulating hepcidin.

Pure red cell aplasia (PRCA) is a rare, life-threatening immunological complication caused by neutralizing anti-erythropoietin antibodies, characterized by sudden severe transfusion-dependent anemia, reticulocyte count < 10,000/mcL, and absent bone marrow erythroblasts.

Erythropoietin resistance (hyporesponsiveness) is diagnosed when patients require high ESA doses without achieving target hemoglobin, most commonly caused by iron deficiency, systemic inflammation/infection, occult gastrointestinal bleeding, or hyperparathyroidism.

modules.name: Hypertension and cardiovascular disease in CKD

topics.title: Hypertension and cardiovascular disease in CKD
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 49; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 57; Harrison 22e Ch. 338

mustKnow.fact: Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of mortality in patients with chronic kidney disease, where non-atherosclerotic mechanisms (arterial stiffness, left ventricular hypertrophy, vascular calcification, and sudden cardiac death) predominate over acute occlusive coronary syndromes.

The 2021 KDIGO Blood Pressure Guideline recommends targeting a standardized office systolic blood pressure < 120 mmHg in CKD patients not on dialysis, supported by evidence from the SPRINT CKD subgroup showing reduced all-cause mortality.

Sodium retention and intravascular volume expansion are the primary hemodynamic drivers of hypertension in chronic kidney disease, causing loss of the normal nocturnal physiological dipping pattern (non-dipping or reverse dipping on 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring).

The CLICK randomized controlled trial demonstrated that the thiazide-like diuretic chlorthalidone significantly reduces 24-hour ambulatory systolic blood pressure by 10.5 mmHg in patients with advanced stage 4 CKD and uncontrolled hypertension.

Uremic cardiomyopathy is characterized pathologically by marked concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, extensive diffuse intermyocardiocytic fibrosis, capillary-to-myocyte mismatch, and diastolic dysfunction.

Resistant hypertension in CKD is defined as blood pressure remaining above target despite concurrent use of three antihypertensive agents of different classes, one of which is an appropriately dosed diuretic.

Troponin T and I concentrations are frequently elevated at baseline in patients with advanced CKD and ESKD due to chronic subclinical myocardial injury and reduced clearance; acute myocardial infarction diagnosis requires acute dynamic rise and fall of cardiac troponin (> 20% delta).

Pericarditis in end-stage kidney disease presents with chest pain and friction rub and is classified as uremic pericarditis (before initiation of maintenance dialysis, responding rapidly to intensive hemodialysis) versus dialysis pericarditis (occurring during established dialysis, often requiring drainage).

topics.title: Renovascular disease
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 50; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 58; Harrison 22e Ch. 339

mustKnow.fact: Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis (ARAS) accounts for 90% of renovascular hypertension cases, typically involving the ostium and proximal third of the main renal artery in older patients with generalized atherosclerotic vascular disease.

Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) accounts for 10% of cases, predominantly affecting young women aged 15 to 50 years, most commonly presenting with medial fibroplasia displaying the classic 'string-of-beads' appearance in the middle and distal renal artery.

The ASTRAL and CORAL randomized controlled trials established that routine renal artery stenting added to comprehensive medical therapy provides no significant benefit in blood pressure control, preservation of renal function, or cardiovascular outcomes in atherosclerotic RAS.

Specific clinical indications for revascularization in renovascular disease include refractory flash pulmonary edema (Pickering syndrome), refractory hypertension resistant to four medications, rapid unexplained loss of kidney function during ACE inhibitor therapy, and bilateral high-grade stenosis.

Percutaneous transluminal renal angioplasty (PTRA) alone without primary stenting is the procedure of choice for fibromuscular dysplasia, achieving technical cure or substantial blood pressure improvement in up to 80% of patients.

Doppler renal ultrasound diagnostic criteria for hemodynamically significant (> 60%) renal artery stenosis include peak systolic velocity (PSV) > 180 to 200 cm/s and renal-to-aortic velocity ratio (RAR) > 3.5.

Atheroembolic renal disease (cholesterol crystal embolization) occurs after vascular catheterization or thrombolytic therapy, presenting with stepwise declining GFR, livedo reticularis, blue toes, hypocomplementemia, peripheral eosinophilia, and biconvex needle-shaped cholesterol clefts on biopsy.

Acute bilateral renal artery occlusion or unilateral occlusion of a single functioning kidney causes acute anuria, severe flank pain, sudden severe hypertension, and markedly elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH).

topics.title: Kidney disease in pregnancy
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 51; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 59; Harrison 22e Ch. 340

mustKnow.fact: Normal gestational renal physiology features a 40% to 50% increase in GFR and effective renal plasma flow driven by relaxin-mediated systemic and renal vasodilation, resulting in lower normal physiological serum creatinine concentrations (0.4 to 0.6 mg/dL).

Preeclampsia is defined as new-onset hypertension (>= 140/90 mmHg) occurring after 20 weeks of gestation accompanied by new proteinuria (>= 300 mg/24h or protein/creatinine ratio >= 0.3 mg/mg) or evidence of maternal end-organ dysfunction.

Pathophysiology of preeclampsia involves defective trophoblastic invasion of uterine spiral arteries with placental hypoxia, triggering excessive release of antiangiogenic factors soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1) and soluble endoglin.

The serum sFlt-1 to placental growth factor (PlGF) ratio (sFlt-1/PlGF ratio <= 38 rule-out threshold) reliably excludes development of preeclampsia within 1 to 4 weeks in women with clinical suspicion.

Kidney biopsy in preeclampsia demonstrates characteristic glomerular endotheliosis, displaying swollen endothelial cells that vacuolate and occlude capillary lumens with loss of endothelial fenestrations without significant immune complex deposition.

First-line antihypertensive medications considered safe for use during pregnancy are oral labetalol, extended-release nifedipine, and methyldopa; ACE inhibitors, ARBs, direct renin inhibitors, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists are strictly fetotoxic and contraindicated.

HELLP syndrome (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) occurs in 10% to 20% of severe preeclampsia, frequently complicated by acute kidney injury and requiring urgent magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis and prompt fetal delivery.

Pregnancy in patients on maintenance hemodialysis requires intensified nocturnal or daily dialysis prescriptions (>= 36 to 48 hours per week) targeting predialysis BUN < 35 to 45 mg/dL to dramatically enhance live birth rates (> 85% to 90%).

topics.title: Drug prescribing in kidney disease
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 52; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 60; Harrison 22e Ch. 341

mustKnow.fact: Kidney clearance of drugs depends on glomerular filtration, tubular secretion (via OCT, OAT, P-glycoprotein), and tubular reabsorption, requiring dosing adjustment based on estimated GFR or creatinine clearance.

The loading dose of a drug depends exclusively on the apparent volume of distribution (Vd) and target plasma concentration, remaining identical in CKD and AKI compared with normal kidney function regardless of clearance.

Maintenance dose adjustments in renal impairment utilize either dose reduction (maintaining normal dosing interval, optimal for time-dependent antibiotics like beta-lactams) or interval extension (maintaining normal dose, preferred for concentration-dependent antibiotics like aminoglycosides).

Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) clearance varies significantly by renal route: dabigatran has 80% renal excretion (contraindicated if CrCl < 30 mL/min), edoxaban 50%, rivaroxaban 33%, and apixaban 27% (lowest renal dependence).
Drug dialyzability during hemodialysis is governed by low molecular weight (< 500 to 1,000 Da), low plasma protein binding (< 80%), small volume of distribution (< 1 L/kg), and high water solubility.

Low-molecular-weight heparins (enoxaparin) depend on renal elimination and accumulate in severe kidney disease (eGFR < 30 mL/min/1.73m2), necessitating dose reduction by 50% or substitution with unfractionated heparin with anti-Xa monitoring.
Cefepime neurotoxicity occurs in unadjusted renal impairment, characterized by altered mental status, myoclonus, choreoathetosis, and non-convulsive status epilepticus with triphasic waves on EEG.

Morphine and meperidine undergo hepatic metabolism into neurotoxic and sedating active metabolites (morphine-6-glucuronide and normeperidine) that accumulate in renal failure; fentanyl and hydromorphone are preferred opioids in CKD.

topics.title: Nutrition and conservative kidney management
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 53-54; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 61; Harrison 22e Ch. 342

mustKnow.fact: Protein-energy wasting (PEW) in CKD is characterized by simultaneous loss of systemic somatic muscle mass and visceral protein reserves, driven by chronic uremic anorexia, persistent low-grade inflammation, and metabolic acidosis.

KDOQI 2020 clinical nutrition guidelines recommend a dietary protein intake of 0.55 to 0.60 g/kg/day (or 0.28 to 0.43 g/kg/day supplemented with essential amino acid ketoacid analogues) for non-dialysis dependent CKD stages 3 to 5.

In contrast to pre-dialysis dietary restriction, maintenance hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis patients require elevated dietary protein intake of 1.0 to 1.2 g/kg/day to compensate for dialytic amino acid and protein losses.

Comprehensive conservative kidney management (CCKM) provides planned, holistic, patient-centered care for advanced CKD without dialysis, focusing on symptom control, advanced care planning, and quality of life.

Studies comparing CCKM with dialysis in frail, highly comorbid elderly patients (age > 75 to 80 years, Charlson Comorbidity Index >= 8) demonstrate equivalent survival duration with fewer hospital days and preserved home time.

Uremic pruritus affects up to 40% to 50% of advanced CKD and dialysis patients, effectively treated by difelikefalin (a selective peripheral kappa-opioid receptor agonist) and gabapentin or pregabalin.

Subjective Global Assessment (SGA) and Malnutrition-Inflammation Score (MIS) are validated multi-component clinical scoring instruments recommended for periodic screening of nutritional status and PEW in CKD.

Restless legs syndrome (RLS) in uremia exhibits strong diurnal exacerbation at night and correlates with peripheral iron deficiency; first-line therapy utilizes low-dose gabapentin, pregabalin, or IV iron replacement.

topics.title: Haemodialysis principles and prescription
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 55; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 62; Harrison 22e Ch. 343

mustKnow.fact: Solute clearance in hemodialysis occurs via diffusion (driven by concentration gradients across semipermeable membrane pores) and convection (solute drag accompanying ultrafiltration driven by transmembrane hydrostatic pressure gradients).

Dialyzer mass transfer area coefficient (KoA, measured in mL/min) reflects membrane permeability and surface area, where high-efficiency dialyzers have KoA > 600 to 800 mL/min for small solutes like urea.

High-flux hemodialysis membranes are defined by an ultrafiltration coefficient (Kuf) > 20 mL/h/mmHg and beta-2 microglobulin clearance > 20 mL/min, achieving superior middle-molecule clearance compared to low-flux membranes.

Hemodiafiltration (HDF) combines high diffusive clearance with high-volume convective fluid exchange (> 23 liters substitution fluid per session in post-dilution mode), reducing cardiovascular and all-cause mortality in the CONVINCE trial.

KDOQI adequacy guidelines recommend a minimum delivered single-pool Kt/V (spKt/V) of 1.2 per session (urea reduction ratio, URR >= 65%) for thrice-weekly hemodialysis, with a target delivered spKt/V of 1.4 (URR 70%).

Standard bicarbonate dialysate composition typically contains sodium 135 to 142 mmol/L, potassium 2.0 to 3.0 mmol/L, calcium 1.25 to 1.50 mmol/L (2.5 to 3.0 mEq/L), magnesium 0.5 mmol/L, and bicarbonate 32 to 38 mmol/L.

Urea rebound occurring 30 to 60 minutes after hemodialysis completion is caused by multi-compartmental solute disequilibrium between intracellular and extracellular fluid spaces, resulting in equilibrated Kt/V (eKt/V) approximately 0.2 units lower than spKt/V.

Reverse osmosis water purification systems must strictly conform to ISO standards for hemodialysis water, ensuring bacterial counts < 100 CFU/mL and endotoxin levels < 0.25 endotoxin units (EU)/mL (ultrapure water < 0.1 CFU/mL and < 0.03 EU/mL).

topics.title: Vascular access for haemodialysis
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 56; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 63; Harrison 22e Ch. 344

mustKnow.fact: Native arteriovenous fistula (AVF) is the preferred permanent vascular access due to superior long-term primary patency and lowest infection, hospitalization, and mortality rates compared to AV grafts and central venous catheters.
The 'Rule of 6s' assesses AVF maturation at 6 weeks post-creation: blood flow > 600 mL/min, vein diameter >= 6 mm, depth <= 6 mm beneath the skin surface, and straight cannulation length >= 6 cm.

Radiocephalic (Brescia-Cimino) fistula at the wrist is the preferred first-line anatomical configuration, followed by brachiocephalic fistula at the elbow and brachiobasilic transposition fistula in the upper arm.

Dialysis access steal syndrome (DASS) manifests as digital coldness, pain during hemodialysis, paresthesias, or distal tissue gangrene due to arterial flow diversion into the low-resistance venous circuit, diagnosed by digital-brachial index (DBI) < 0.6.

DRIL procedure (Distal Revascularization and Interval Ligation) is the definitive surgical management of severe access-induced ischemia, creating a bypass graft to the distal artery and ligating the native artery immediately distal to the fistula anastomosis.

Arteriovenous graft (AVG, typically expanded polytetrafluoroethylene, ePTFE) has higher primary failure rates than AVF and is prone to thrombosis secondary to neointimal venous anastomotic stenosis driven by turbulent shear stress and smooth muscle proliferation.

Catheter-related bloodstream infection (CRBSI) in tunneled cuffed internal jugular catheters requires empirical systemic broad-spectrum antibiotics covering Staphylococcus aureus (vancomycin) and Gram-negative bacilli (cefepime or aminoglycoside), with catheter removal indicated for tunnel infection, septic shock, or metastatic complications.

Subclavian vein catheterization is strictly avoided for hemodialysis vascular access due to a 30% to 50% incidence of severe subclavian vein stenosis that permanently precludes ipsilateral arm AVF or AVG creation.

topics.title: Complications of haemodialysis
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 57; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 64; Harrison 22e Ch. 345

mustKnow.fact: Intradialytic hypotension (IDH), defined as a systolic blood pressure drop >= 20 mmHg or mean arterial pressure drop >= 10 mmHg with clinical symptoms, is the most frequent acute complication of hemodialysis, occurring in 15% to 20% of sessions.

Ultrafiltration rate (UFR) exceeding 13 mL/kg/h is independently associated with significant myocardial stunning, cerebral ischemia, mesenteric hypoperfusion, and increased all-cause and cardiovascular mortality.

Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome (DDS) is a life-threatening neurological complication occurring during or after aggressive initial hemodialysis in patients with severe azotemia (BUN > 150 mg/dL), driven by reverse osmotic cerebral edema from rapid extracellular urea clearance.

Prevention of DDS in initiating hemodialysis requires limiting initial treatment duration to 2.0 to 2.5 hours, keeping blood flow rate low (150 to 200 mL/min), and targeting a modest urea reduction of <= 30% to 40%.

Type A first-use hypersensitivity reaction occurs within minutes of initiating hemodialysis, mediated by IgE antibodies to ethylene oxide sterilant or AN69 dialyzer membranes in patients taking ACE inhibitors, requiring immediate circuit clamp without returning blood.

Type B first-use reaction manifests 20 to 40 minutes into hemodialysis with chest and back pain caused by complement activation (C3a, C5a) on contact with cellulosic membranes, generally resolving spontaneously with continued treatment.

Dialysis-related amyloidosis is caused by systemic tissue deposition of beta-2 microglobulin amyloid fibrils in patients on long-term hemodialysis (> 10 years), presenting as bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, flexor tenosynovitis, and subchondral bone cysts.

Acquired cystic kidney disease (ACKD) develops in 50% of patients on hemodialysis for > 3 years and > 80% after 10 years, carrying a 3- to 6-fold increased risk of renal cell carcinoma (most commonly clear cell and papillary RCC).

topics.title: Peritoneal dialysis
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 58-59; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 65; Harrison 22e Ch. 346

mustKnow.fact: Rippe's three-pore model of peritoneal transport comprises ultrasmall aquaporin-1 pores (radius < 0.5 nm, water-only transport without solute, mediating 50% of transcapillary ultrafiltration during hypertonic dwells), small pores (radius 4 to 5 nm, mediating small-solute diffusion), and large pores (radius > 20 nm, mediating protein leak).

The standard Peritoneal Equilibration Test (PET) classifies membrane solute transport using a 4-hour 2.27% (or 2.5%) dextrose dwell into four categories: high (dialysate-to-plasma creatinine ratio D/P Cr > 0.81), high-average (0.65 to 0.81), low-average (0.50 to 0.64), and low (< 0.50).

High peritoneal transporters rapidly dissipate the osmotic glucose gradient leading to early fluid reabsorption and poor ultrafiltration on continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD); they are optimally managed with automated peritoneal dialysis (APD) with short dwell times and daytime icodextrin.

Icodextrin is a high-molecular-weight glucose polymer (average molecular weight 13,000 to 19,000 Da) that produces sustained colloid osmosis across small pores during long daytime or overnight dwells, overcoming glucose-induced ultrafiltration failure.

ISPD guideline adequacy targets for peritoneal dialysis focus on clinical wellness, euvolemia, and symptom management, recommending a total (peritoneal plus residual kidney) Kt/V urea of at least 1.7 per week when adequacy is assessed numerically.

Preservation of residual kidney function (RKF) is superior in peritoneal dialysis compared to hemodialysis and provides vital survival, fluid balance, and middle-molecule clearance advantages, protected by avoidance of nephrotoxic drugs and maintenance of euvolemia.

Sodium sieving refers to the fall in dialysate sodium concentration during the first 60 to 90 minutes of a hypertonic dextrose dwell, reflecting exclusive free water transport through aquaporin-1 channels; a drop < 5 mmol/L confirms aquaporin-1 deficiency.

Encapsulating peritoneal sclerosis (EPS) is a rare catastrophic complication associated with long PD duration (> 5 to 8 years) and recurrent peritonitis, characterized by dense collagenous peritoneal fibrovascular encasement causing intestinal cocooning and mechanical obstruction.

modules.name: Peritoneal dialysis peritonitis and catheter infections

topics.title: Peritoneal dialysis peritonitis and catheter infections
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 60; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 66; Harrison 22e Ch. 347

mustKnow.fact: The 2022 ISPD guidelines define peritoneal dialysis peritonitis by the presence of at least two of three criteria: clinical features of peritonitis (cloudy effluent, abdominal pain); effluent leukocyte count > 100/mcL with > 50% polymorphonuclear cells; and positive effluent culture.

Empirical antimicrobial therapy must be initiated immediately upon diagnosing cloudy effluent, incorporating intraperitoneal coverage for both Gram-positive organisms (vancomycin or a first-generation cephalosporin like cefazolin) and Gram-negative organisms (ceftazidime or an aminoglycoside).

Refractory peritonitis is defined as failure of peritoneal effluent to clear after 5 days of appropriate antibiotic therapy, mandating prompt PD catheter removal to preserve the peritoneal membrane and prevent sepsis and death.

Relapsing peritonitis is an episode occurring within 4 weeks of completing therapy for a prior episode with the same organism, whereas recurrent peritonitis occurs within 4 weeks with a different organism.

Fungal peritonitis (most frequently Candida albicans or Candida parapsilosis) mandates immediate, mandatory PD catheter removal alongside systemic antifungal therapy (amphotericin B, fluconazole, or echinocandins) due to biofilm colonization.

Enteric peritonitis yielding multiple enteric Gram-negative organisms (or mixed anaerobes and Gram-negatives) strongly raises suspicion for secondary surgical peritonitis from intra-abdominal pathology (diverticulitis, ischemic bowel, perforated viscus).

Catheter exit-site infection is diagnosed by purulent drainage at the skin-catheter interface; topical antibacterial prophylaxis with daily exit-site mupirocin cream or gentamicin cream significantly reduces exit-site infections and catheter-related peritonitis.

Oral antibiotic prophylaxis with a single dose of amoxicillin-clavulanic acid or ampicillin with aminoglycoside is strongly recommended prior to invasive colonoscopic or gynecologic procedures in patients on peritoneal dialysis.

topics.title: Transplant immunology and histocompatibility
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 76; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 67; Harrison 22e Ch. 348

mustKnow.fact: Direct allorecognition occurs when recipient T cell receptors directly bind intact intact donor intact MHC molecules on donor passenger dendritic cells, driving vigorous acute cellular rejection; indirect allorecognition involves recipient antigen-presenting cells processing donor MHC peptides, mediating chronic antibody-mediated rejection.

Complement-dependent cytotoxicity (CDC) crossmatch detects cytotoxic anti-donor HLA antibodies: a positive T-cell CDC crossmatch represents an absolute contraindication to transplantation due to inevitable hyperacute rejection.

Flow cytometric crossmatch (FCXM) is 10- to 100-fold more sensitive than CDC for detecting low-titer non-complement-fixing anti-HLA antibodies, predicting early graft dysfunction and acute rejection episodes.

Luminex single-antigen bead (SAB) assays identify donor-specific anti-HLA antibodies (DSA) and quantify mean fluorescence intensity (MFI), where MFI thresholds > 1,000 to 5,000 define clinically relevant immunological risk.

Calculated Panel Reactive Antibody (cPRA) expresses the percentage of deceased donors in a donor pool who express HLA antigens against which the candidate has unacceptable antibodies, reflecting the difficulty of finding a compatible organ.

T cell activation requires three signals: Signal 1 (TCR engagement of MHC-peptide), Signal 2 (costimulation, primarily CD28 binding CD80/CD86, blocked by belatacept), and Signal 3 (IL-2 receptor activation triggering mTOR, blocked by basiliximab and mTOR inhibitors).

ABO-incompatible kidney transplantation requires pre-transplant desensitization using B-cell depletion (rituximab), antigen removal via plasmapheresis or immunoadsorption, and intravenous immunoglobulin, targeting anti-A/B isoagglutinin titers <= 1:8 to 1:16 at transplantation.

Imlifidase (IdeS) is a recombinant IgG-degrading cysteine endopeptidase derived from Streptococcus pyogenes that rapidly cleaves all human IgG subclasses at the hinge region into F(ab')2 and Fc fragments within 2 to 6 hours, enabling successful desensitization and transplantation in highly sensitized cPRA 100% patients.

topics.title: Donor and recipient evaluation
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 77; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 68; Harrison 22e Ch. 349

mustKnow.fact: Living kidney donor evaluation requires a rigorously measured GFR >= 90 mL/min/1.73m2 (or >= 80 mL/min/1.73m2 in selected older donors), normal 24-hour urine albumin (< 30 mg/day), and comprehensive cardiovascular and psychosocial clearance.

Long-term prospective registry studies demonstrate that donor nephrectomy causes a mild increase in lifetime risk of end-stage kidney disease (absolute risk approximately 0.5% to 1.0% at 15 years, compared to 0.1% in healthy non-donors).

The Kidney Donor Profile Index (KDPI) calculates deceased donor organ quality as a percentile score from 0% to 100% relative to all deceased donors recovered in the prior year; KDPI > 85% identifies high-risk extended criteria organs associated with shorter graft survival.

Donation after circulatory death (DCD) kidneys experience prolonged warm ischemia time during the agonal period between withdrawal of life support and cold perfusion, resulting in delayed graft function (DGF) rates of 40% to 60%.

Hypothermic machine perfusion (HMP) of deceased donor kidneys significantly reduces the incidence of delayed graft function and improves 1-year and 3-year graft survival compared with static cold storage.

Paired kidney exchange (kidney paired donation, KPD) overcomes immunological incompatibility (positive crossmatch or ABO incompatibility) between a living donor and recipient by swapping donors with other incompatible pairs.

Preemptive kidney transplantation (transplantation performed before the initiation of maintenance dialysis) provides the best long-term graft and patient survival, reduced cardiovascular morbidity, and significant health-economic savings.

Transplantation of kidneys from hepatitis C virus (HCV) viremic donors into HCV-negative recipients followed by early post-transplant direct-acting antiviral (DAA) therapy achieves > 95% to 100% sustained virological cure and excellent graft function.

topics.title: Immunosuppressive therapy
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 78; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 69; Harrison 22e Ch. 350

mustKnow.fact: T-cell depleting induction therapy with rabbit antithymocyte globulin (rATG, 1.5 mg/kg/day for 3 to 5 doses) is strongly indicated for recipients at high immunological risk (high cPRA, repeat transplant, presence of DSA, black race), while basiliximab (anti-IL-2R alpha) is preferred in standard-risk recipients.

Tacrolimus binds intracellular FKBP12 to inhibit calcineurin phosphatase, preventing dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of NFAT; maintaining whole-blood trough levels between 8 and 12 ng/mL in the first 3 months, then 5 to 8 ng/mL thereafter.

The ELITE-Symphony trial established that low-dose tacrolimus combined with mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), corticosteroids, and daclizumab induction provides superior allograft function, lower acute rejection rates, and better graft survival compared to cyclosporine or sirolimus.

Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF 1,000 mg twice daily) is a prodrug of mycophenolic acid (MPA), which selectively and reversibly inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH), blocking de novo purine nucleotide synthesis in proliferating T and B lymphocytes.

Belatacept is a soluble recombinant fusion protein (CTLA-4 linked to modified Fc of human IgG1) that selectively blocks CD28 costimulation by binding CD80/CD86, avoiding calcineurin inhibitor nephrotoxicity and improving long-term eGFR in the BENEFIT trials.

Belatacept is strictly contraindicated in recipients who are Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) seronegative due to a markedly increased risk of post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD), predominantly affecting the central nervous system.

mTOR inhibitors (sirolimus, everolimus) bind FKBP12 to inhibit mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1), but side effects include impaired wound healing, incisional hernia, pneumonitis, hyperlipidemia, and new-onset proteinuria.

Calcineurin inhibitors and mTOR inhibitors undergo extensive hepatic and intestinal metabolism by cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) and P-glycoprotein; CYP3A4 inhibitors (azole antifungals, diltiazem, macrolides) markedly elevate levels, while inducers (rifampin, phenytoin, St. John's wort) precipitate acute rejection.

topics.title: Allograft rejection and dysfunction
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 79; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 70; Harrison 22e Ch. 351

mustKnow.fact: Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes to hours of vascular clamp release, mediated by pre-existing complement-fixing anti-donor ABO or HLA class I antibodies causing diffuse thrombotic occlusion and graft necrosis.

The Banff classification categorizes T-cell mediated rejection (TCMR) by interstitial inflammation ('i' score) and tubulitis ('t' score): Grade IA (i2/i3 and t2), Grade IB (i2/i3 and t3), Grade IIA/IIB (arterial intimal arteritis, 'v1' and 'v2'), and Grade III (transmural arteritis, 'v3').

Acute antibody-mediated rejection (AMR) requires three Banff criteria: acute tissue injury (microvascular inflammation, glomerulitis 'g' and peritubular capillaritis 'ptc'), evidence of recent antibody interaction (linear C4d staining in >= 10% of peritubular capillaries), and circulating donor-specific anti-HLA antibodies (DSA).

First-line therapy for acute cellular rejection is intravenous pulse methylprednisolone (500 mg daily for 3 days), escalating to lymphocyte-depleting rabbit antithymocyte globulin (rATG) for steroid-resistant rejection or Banff Grade II/III vascular rejection.

Acute antibody-mediated rejection is treated with multimodal therapy including therapeutic plasma exchange (PEX) to remove circulating DSA, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), and anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody (rituximab) or proteasome inhibitor (bortezomib).

Chronic active antibody-mediated rejection manifests pathologically as transplant glomerulopathy (cg score > 0, double contours of glomerular basement membrane) and multilamination of peritubular capillary basement membranes.

Donor-derived cell-free DNA (dd-cfDNA) in recipient blood serves as a non-invasive liquid biopsy biomarker; a dd-cfDNA fraction > 0.5% to 1.0% accurately differentiates acute allograft rejection from calcineurin inhibitor toxicity and stable graft function.

Interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy (IFTA) on protocol allograft biopsy reflects chronic cumulative damage from immune rejection, chronic calcineurin inhibitor nephrotoxicity, hypertension, and recurrent viral infections.

topics.title: Infections after kidney transplantation
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 80; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 71; Harrison 22e Ch. 352

mustKnow.fact: Fishman's timeline of post-transplant infections defines three distinct periods: Month 1 (hospital-acquired bacterial/surgical infections), Months 1 to 6 (opportunistic viral infections: CMV, EBV, BK virus, and Pneumocystis), and beyond Month 6 (community-acquired pathogens).

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) transmission risk is highest in donor-positive/recipient-negative (D+/R-) mismatches, mandating 6 months of universal antiviral prophylaxis with oral valganciclovir (900 mg once daily, renal-adjusted), compared to 3 months in CMV-seropositive recipients.

Letermovir, a viral terminase complex inhibitor that does not cause bone marrow suppression, is effective for CMV prophylaxis, while maribavir (inhibitor of UL97 protein kinase) is approved for refractory or ganciclovir-resistant CMV infection.

Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) prophylaxis with daily single-strength oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX 80/400 mg) is standard for at least 6 to 12 months post-transplant and throughout treatment for acute rejection.

Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD) is predominantly driven by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), displaying greatest incidence in EBV-seronegative recipients receiving an EBV-seropositive allograft (D+/R-).

Tuberculosis in renal transplant recipients presents atypically with disseminated, miliary, or extrapulmonary disease in over 50% of cases, requiring rifabutin in place of rifampin to avoid severe induction of calcineurin inhibitor clearance.

Invasive fungal infections (Aspergillus fumigatus, Cryptococcus neoformans, Mucorales) occur during periods of intensified immunosuppression, where azole antifungals (voriconazole, posaconazole) dramatically increase tacrolimus and cyclosporine levels via CYP3A4 inhibition.
Live attenuated vaccines (MMR, varicella, yellow fever, oral polio) are strictly contraindicated in solid organ transplant recipients on immunosuppressive therapy.

topics.title: BK polyomavirus nephropathy
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 81; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 72; Harrison 22e Ch. 353

mustKnow.fact: BK polyomavirus is a double-stranded circular DNA virus that resides latently in recipient and donor renal tubular epithelial and urothelial cells, reactivating under potent immunosuppression (particularly tacrolimus and MMF regimens).
Decoy cells are urothelial cells with characteristic ground-glass, enlarged basophilic intranuclear viral inclusion bodies, detectable in urine cytology during early BK viruria.

KDIGO guidelines recommend routine screening for BK virus replication with plasma quantitative PCR monthly for the first 3 to 6 months post-transplant, then every 3 months until 12 months, and whenever serum creatinine unexplainedly rises.
Presumptive BK polyomavirus nephropathy is diagnosed when plasma BK viral load remains persistently >= 10^4 copies/mL (or >= 4.0 log10 copies/mL) for at least 3 weeks.

Definitive diagnosis of BK polyomavirus nephropathy (BKPyVN) requires allograft biopsy demonstrating intranuclear viral inclusions, tubulitis, interstitial inflammation, and positive immunohistochemical nuclear staining for SV40 large T antigen.

Primary cornerstone of therapy for BKPyVN is stepwise reduction of maintenance immunosuppression (reducing MMF by 50% or stopping it completely, followed by lowering calcineurin inhibitor trough targets by 25% to 50%).

Adjunctive second-line therapies evaluated for refractory BK viremia include leflunomide (an active metabolite inhibitor of pyrimidine synthesis with antiviral properties), intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), and cidofovir.

Late complications of BK virus replication in the urinary tract include ureteric stenosis, ulceration, and obstruction secondary to dense viral-induced inflammation and scarring, as well as hemorrhagic cystitis.

topics.title: Medical complications after transplantation
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 82-83; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 73; Harrison 22e Ch. 354

mustKnow.fact: New-onset diabetes after transplantation (NODAT / PTDM) develops in 15% to 30% of recipients, primarily driven by tacrolimus-induced beta-cell toxicity and corticosteroid-induced insulin resistance.

Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the skin is the most common post-transplant malignancy, occurring with a 65- to 250-fold increased incidence compared to the general population and displaying aggressive biological behavior with high metastatic potential.

Post-transplant erythrocytosis (PTE, hematocrit > 51% in males or > 48% in females) occurs in 10% to 15% of patients with well-functioning allografts, mediated by endogenous erythropoietin and renin-angiotensin overproduction, responding effectively to ACE inhibitors or ARBs.

Transplant renal artery stenosis (TRAS) typically develops within the first 6 to 12 months at or near the arterial anastomosis, presenting with refractory hypertension and acute rise in serum creatinine upon starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB.

Primary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) recurs in 30% to 50% of first kidney transplants (up to > 80% in second grafts), manifesting as heavy nephrotic proteinuria within hours to days post-surgery, treatable with urgent plasma exchange.

Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) carries a 60% to 80% risk of post-transplant recurrence in patients with pathogenic complement factor H (CFH) mutations; prophylactic complement C5 inhibition with eculizumab or ravulizumab successfully prevents allograft loss.

Periallograft lymphocele occurs in up to 15% to 20% of kidney transplants, caused by divided recipient pelvic or donor iliac lymphatics; significant collections causing ureteral compression or leg edema are treated with laparoscopic peritoneal fenestration (marsupialization).

Persistent post-transplant tertiary hyperparathyroidism occurs in up to 30% to 50% of recipients due to autonomous parathyroid gland hyperplasia, causing hypercalcemia and hypophosphatemia, managed medically with cinacalcet or surgically with subtotal parathyroidectomy.

topics.title: Onconephrology
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 84; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 74; Harrison 22e Ch. 355

mustKnow.fact: Cairo-Bishop diagnostic criteria for laboratory tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) require two or more of: uric acid >= 8.0 mg/dL, potassium >= 6.0 mmol/L, phosphorus >= 4.5 mg/dL, and calcium <= 7.0 mg/dL (or 25% change from baseline) within 3 to 7 days of chemotherapy.

Rasburicase (recombinant urate oxidase, 0.15 to 0.20 mg/kg or fixed single dose 3 to 6 mg) enzymatically degrades uric acid to allantoin (5 to 10 times more soluble in urine), but is strictly contraindicated in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency due to severe methemoglobinemia and hemolysis.

Immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated acute kidney injury (CPI-AKI, incidence 3% to 5%) is most commonly caused by PD-1/PD-L1 or CTLA-4 inhibitors (pembrolizumab, nivolumab, ipilimumab), presenting histopathologically as acute tubulointerstitial nephritis.

Management of grade 2 or higher checkpoint inhibitor-induced AKI requires withholding the immune checkpoint inhibitor and initiating oral prednisone (0.5 to 1.0 mg/kg/day), with complete rechallenge permitted only after renal recovery to baseline.

Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) pathway inhibitors (bevacizumab, sunitinib, lenvatinib) disrupt podocyte-derived VEGF-A cross-talk with glomerular endothelial VEGFR2, causing new or worsening hypertension and renal thrombotic microangiopathy with proteinuria.

High-dose methotrexate (> 500 mg/m2) precipitates as yellow-orange insoluble crystals within renal tubular lumens at acid pH, preventing excretion and inducing acute crystalline nephropathy; prevention requires aggressive intravenous hydration and urinary alkalinization (urine pH >= 7.0).

Glucarpidase (carboxypeptidase G2) is an emergency rescue recombinant bacterial enzyme that rapidly cleaves extracellular methotrexate into inactive metabolites (DAMPA and glutamate) within 15 minutes, indicated in high-dose methotrexate toxicity with acute renal failure.

Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy causes cytokine release syndrome (CRS) with massive IL-6 release, systemic vasodilation, capillary leak, and severe prerenal and acute tubular injury, effectively reversed by the anti-IL-6 receptor antagonist tocilizumab.

topics.title: HIV and viral hepatitis-associated kidney disease
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 85; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 75; Harrison 22e Ch. 356

mustKnow.fact: HIV-associated nephropathy (HIVAN) is characterized histopathologically by a rapidly progressive collapsing variant of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, accompanied by microcystic tubular dilatation containing proteinaceous casts and diffuse tubulointerstitial inflammation.

HIVAN occurs almost exclusively in individuals of African ancestry carrying two APOL1 risk alleles (G1/G1, G2/G2, or G1/G2), driven by direct productive HIV infection of podocytes and tubular epithelial cells expressing viral genes nef and vpr.

HIV immune complex kidney disease (HIVICK) accounts for a major proportion of kidney disease in virally suppressed HIV patients on antiretroviral therapy, presenting with immune-complex mediated MPGN or lupus-like glomerulonephritis without collapsing features.

Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) causes proximal renal tubular mitochondrial toxicity via human organic anion transporter 1 (OAT1) accumulation, manifesting as Fanconi syndrome with hypophosphatemia, glucosuria, and declining GFR; substituted by tenofovir alafenamide (TAF).

Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is most characteristically associated with secondary membranous nephropathy (predominantly in children and young adults mediated by HBeAg subepithelial deposition) and classical polyarteritis nodosa (PAN).

Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is classically associated with Type II mixed cryoglobulinemia, presenting with the Meltzer triad (palpable purpura, arthralgias, asthenia), marked hypocomplementemia with profoundly low C4, and MPGN with intracapillary IgM-kappa cryoglobulin thrombi.

Direct-acting antivirals (DAAs: glecaprevir-pibrentasvir, sofosbuvir-velpatasvir) achieve sustained virological response (SVR > 95% to 98%) in HCV-associated cryoglobulinemic MPGN, achieving clinical renal remission and clearing cryoglobulins.

COVID-19-associated nephropathy (COVAN) is a collapsing glomerulopathy presenting with heavy proteinuria and acute kidney injury in patients with high-risk APOL1 genotypes, triggered by SARS-CoV-2-induced robust interferon-gamma and chemokine release.

topics.title: Poisoning and extracorporeal therapies
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 86; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 76; Harrison 22e Ch. 357

mustKnow.fact: The EXTRIP (Extracorporeal Treatments in Poisoning) workgroup criteria recommend hemodialysis for severe lithium toxicity when serum lithium > 4.0 mmol/L (or > 2.5 mmol/L with severe neurologic manifestations, altered consciousness, or kidney failure).

Methanol poisoning causes severe high anion gap metabolic acidosis and elevated osmolar gap through metabolism by alcohol dehydrogenase to toxic formic acid, which inhibits cytochrome oxidase causing optic papillitis, blindness, and bilateral putaminal necrosis.

Ethylene glycol poisoning produces calcium oxalate monohydrate crystal deposition throughout renal tubules and cerebral vessels, caused by glycolic acid and oxalic acid accumulation, presenting with flank pain, acute tubular necrosis, and hypocalcemia.

Fomepizole (4-methylpyrazole, 15 mg/kg loading dose) is a potent competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase that prevents toxic metabolite formation in methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning, administered alongside immediate hemodialysis for severe acidemia (pH < 7.15).

Severe salicylate (aspirin) toxicity is treated with urgent hemodialysis when serum salicylate levels exceed 90 mg/dL (6.5 mmol/L) in acute ingestion, or > 60 mg/dL in chronic poisoning with altered mental status, severe acidemia, or pulmonary edema.

EXTRIP recommendations for metformin-associated lactic acidosis (MALA) endorse intermittent hemodialysis for severe refractory lactic acidosis (lactate > 20 mmol/L, pH <= 7.00, or failure of standard supportive therapy).

Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) is recommended as Category I indication by ASFA guidelines for thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), anti-GBM disease with pulmonary hemorrhage, and ANCA vasculitis with alveolar hemorrhage.

Extracorporeal removal via hemoperfusion or hemodialysis is ineffective for intoxicants with large volume of distribution (> 2 to 3 L/kg, e.g., tricyclic antidepressants, digoxin, chloroquine) or high tissue binding.

topics.title: Paediatric nephrology essentials
topics.book: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology 7e Ch. 87; Brenner & Rector 11e Ch. 77; Nelson Pediatrics 22e Ch. 545

mustKnow.fact: Idiopathic nephrotic syndrome in children is steroid-sensitive (SSNS) in > 85% to 90% of cases, with minimal change disease representing the underlying histology in over 80% of childhood presentations between ages 1 and 6 years.

Steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS) in infants and young children is caused by monogenic podocyte gene mutations in up to 30% of cases, most frequently involving NPHS1 (nephrin), NPHS2 (podocin), WT1, and LAMB2.

Congenital nephrotic syndrome of the Finnish type (CNF) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by bi-allelic mutations in NPHS1 (encoding nephrin), presenting with massive in utero proteinuria, huge placenta (> 25% of birth weight), and severe nephrotic syndrome at birth.

Denys-Drash syndrome is caused by dominant point mutations in the zinc-finger region of the WT1 gene (exon 8 or 9), characterized by the triad of early-onset diffuse mesangial sclerosis (DMS), male pseudohermaphroditism (XY disorder of sex development), and high risk of Wilms tumor.

Frasier syndrome is caused by alternative donor splice site mutations in intron 9 of the WT1 gene, presenting with late-onset steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome with FSGS histology, complete male sex reversal (46,XY females), and gonadoblastoma.

Posterior urethral valves (PUV) represent the most common cause of congenital lower urinary tract obstruction in male infants, diagnosed antenatally by bilateral hydroureteronephrosis, distended thick-walled bladder ('keyhole sign'), and oligohydramnios.

Childhood hypertension is defined statistically by systolic or diastolic blood pressure >= 95th percentile for age, sex, and height on three or more occasions, with renal parenchymal disease (glomerulonephritis, reflux nephropathy) representing the leading secondary cause.

Primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis in children >= 5 years of age is driven by nocturnal polyuria (decreased nocturnal vasopressin secretion), nocturnal detrusor overactivity, and failure to awaken; first-line therapy incorporates enuresis alarm training and oral desmopressin (melt formulation).
